title: Shopping with a Platform AI Assistant: Who Adopts, When in the Journey, and What for
affiliations: Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management,  and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Shopping with a Platform AI Assistant: Who Adopts, When in the Journey, and What for
detail.abstract: This paper provides some of the first large-scale descriptive evidence on how consumers adopt and use platform-embedded shopping AI in e-commerce. Using data on 31 million users of Ctrip, China's largest online travel platform, we study "Wendao," an LLM-based AI assistant integrated into the platform. We document three empirical regularities. First, adoption is highest among older consumers, female users, and highly engaged existing users, reversing the younger, male-dominated profile commonly documented for general-purpose AI tools. Second, AI chat appears in the same broad phase of the purchase journey as traditional search and well before order placement; among journeys containing both chat and search, the most common pattern is interleaving, with users moving back and forth between the two modalities. Third, consumers disproportionately use the assistant for exploratory, hard-to-keyword tasks: attraction queries account for 42% of observed chat requests, and chat intent varies systematically with both the timing of chat relative to search and the category of products later purchased within the same journey. These findings suggest that embedded shopping AI functions less as a substitute for conventional search than as a complementary interface for exploratory product discovery in e-commerce.

detail.abstract:
The forty-hour working week was never an efficiency optimum. It was a coordination device built for the industrial economy, and artificial intelligence is dissolving the conditions that made it work.

This paper argues that the primary risk of AI-driven automation is not technological but macroeconomic. As AI severs the relationship between time input and value output across knowledge-intensive sectors, productivity gains are concentrating in returns to capital while professional labour income contracts. The result is a coordination failure: firms that extract maximum efficiency from AI while reducing their wage base are individually rational and collectively self-defeating, systematically removing spending power from the markets they depend on.

The paper identifies this dynamic as the demand problem that current AI discourse is not naming clearly enough, examines why markets will not resolve it spontaneously, and sets out a staged transition toward value-based work, organised around human judgment, accountability, and creative synthesis rather than time. It draws on evidence from labour market research, institutional economics, and governance practice to argue that this transition is a macroeconomic necessity, not a lifestyle preference.

The implications for boards are direct. AI workforce strategy is a material financial risk that belongs on the audit and risk agenda, not an ESG consideration or a communications challenge. The coordination failure will eventually produce a regulatory response. The question is whether organisations are positioned ahead of it or behind it.

detail.title: "Under A Carolina Sky"
detail.abstract: Abstract With increases in firms’ deployment of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) agents with the capacity to converse with customers, research on the impact of CAI on brand equity has been rising. However, a gap exists on comprehensive insights into how various characteristics of CAI impact different facets of brand equity. Through a systematic literature review of 42 refereed research articles that reported empirical research findings on this topic, this study identified 16 CAI characteristic constructs of which relationships to one or more of eight customer-level brand equity constructs examined in the current CAI literature. Further, this review revealed significant literature gaps in the impact of CAI use on market- and financiallevel brand equity as well as needs for further investigations on how CAI skill and identity characteristics affect the attitudinal and behavioral dimensions of customer-level brand equity. Our findings are expected to stimulate future research while offering valuable guidance to industry practitioners seeking to integrate CAI into customer encounters.

detail.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) raises productivity inside jobs while reducing the informativeness of the screening outputs used to allocate workers across firms. In a stylized matching model, the market sorts efficiently on visible rank, but rank is an imperfect proxy for worker type. Aggregate output, decomposed into average worker output and a misallocation penalty, can therefore fall even when every worker-firm pair becomes more productive. The analysis predicts weaker screening validity, greater use of harder-to-fake assessments, socially excessive applicant AI use as well as greater reliance on probationary hiring and rematching. Empirical design suggestions to test these predictions are provided.

title: Baqqla and the Buyer-Initiated Reverse Marketplace: A Market Design Approach to Search Costs, Price Discovery, and Advertising Waste in E-Commerce SSRN Working Paper Draft Conceptual Article

detail.title: Baqqla and the Buyer-Initiated Reverse Marketplace: A Market Design Approach to Search Costs, Price Discovery, and Advertising Waste in E-Commerce SSRN Working Paper Draft Conceptual Article
detail.abstract: This article conceptualizes Baqqla as a buyer-initiated reverse marketplace, a platform architecture that reverses the dominant seller-led logic of contemporary e-commerce. In conventional online marketplaces, sellers list products and buyers search across large sets of alternatives under conditions of incomplete information, ranking distortions, and persistent price dispersion. In Baqqla's proposed model, buyers initiate the transaction by posting a structured request, after which sellers compete by submitting visible offers along multiple dimensions such as price, delivery, warranty, and bundled benefits. The article positions this mechanism at the intersection of the economics of information, auction theory, two-sided platform economics, and market design. Conceptually, Baqqla resembles a reverse auction or procurement auction, but differs in three key respects: it is adapted to business-to-consumer commerce, it relies on open rather than sealed competition, and it supports multidimensional rather than price-only rivalry. The central argument is that a buyer-initiated reverse marketplace may reduce buyer search costs, improve comparative decision quality, and substitute transaction-contingent competition for part of the waste associated with advertising-led customer acquisition. Because platformspecific outcomes have not yet been empirically established, the article advances a set of theoretically grounded propositions for future testing rather than making causal claims about realized welfare gains.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Small Open Economy: Structural Adaptation, Institutional Constraints, and Strategic Options for New Zealand

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Small Open Economy: Structural Adaptation, Institutional Constraints, and Strategic Options for New Zealand
detail.abstract: New Zealand presents an instructive case study in the challenges confronting small, open, commodity-dependent economies as artificial intelligence reshapes global production, trade, and employment. The country derives over half of total exports from food and fibre-principally dairy, meat, forestry, and horticulture-and a further substantial share from tourism, yet simultaneously hosts a rapidly growing technology sector contributing NZ$23.8 billion (8% of GDP) and advanced digital infrastructure including hyperscale cloud investments exceeding NZ$15 billion from Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, and Google. This paper synthesises evidence from over 120 sources across economics, technology policy, agricultural science, indigenous governance, and comparative political economy to assess New Zealand's vulnerabilities and strategic options in the AI transition. We find that institutional projections of AI's economic impact range from Acemoglu's estimate of 0.53-0.66% total factor productivity growth over a decade to McKinsey's projection of US$17-26 trillion in annual value creation, and that New Zealand's national AI strategy-released in July 2025 as the last among OECD members-adopts an adoption-focused, light-touch approach that may prove insufficient given the scale of disruption that even conservative estimates imply. Comparative analysis of Singapore, Ireland, Estonia, Israel, and the Nordic countries reveals that successful small-economy AI strategies share three features: high-level government coordination, deep sectoral specialisation, and investment at scale relative to GDP. We identify four domains where New Zealand's natural advantages-85-96% renewable electricity, world-leading pastoral agricultural technology, Treaty of Waitangi-based indigenous governance frameworks, and established creative technology clusters-intersect with AI opportunity, while documenting critical constraints including a 68% reported AI graduate emigration rate (from a single advocacy source whose methodology warrants scrutiny), fiscal austerity that renders large-scale public investment improbable under current settings, and grid capacity limitations that complicate the renewable computing narrative. We propose several novel strategic concepts, including the reframing of emigrant talent as a distributed asset network rather than a loss, the development of indigenous data governance standards as a globally licensable product, and hyper-specialisation across 20-30 micro-niches rather than competition in broad AI domains. The analysis suggests that New Zealand's path lies not in replicating the institutional models of Singapore or Israel-whose structural conditions differ fundamentally-but in developing market-compatible, fiscally realistic mechanisms that exploit the country's distinctive advantages while acknowledging the binding constraints of a small, geographically remote economy operating under tight fiscal conditions.

detail.abstract: This paper systematically evaluates the academic and corporate literature to present a taxonomy of marketing use cases based on machine learning. We identify eleven common use cases that fall into four distinct groups reflecting the core areas of leverage for machine learning in marketing: shopper fundamentals, consuming experience, decisions, and financial impact. We then present a unified framework and a multi-faceted agenda for incorporating machine learning methods into academic marketing research. The framework contains five key components of empirical research: method, data, issue, usage, and theory. By examining each component and its interactions with the others, we derive a comprehensive research agenda that aims to help bridge the gap between practice and academia in applying machine learning to marketing problems.

title: Intelligent Talent Systems (ITS): A Structural, Non-Reifying Architecture for Governing the Human-Institution Interface

The work is theoretical and conceptual in nature and does not evaluate, promote, or assess any commercial product, service, or organization.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently as part of a broader conceptual and theoretical research program on institutional design, governance, and human–system interaction.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary talent, performance, and capability systems continue to individualize institutional failure. Burnout, ethical drift, leadership collapse, and organizational brittleness are routinely explained through traits, competencies, or resilience deficits, obscuring the role of misdesigned structures, overloaded roles, and absent governance. This paper introduces Intelligent Talent Systems (ITS), a multi-layered conceptual architecture for governing the human–institution interface without reifying individuals into fixed types, latent capabilities, or predictive scores.


ITS is grounded in a strict ontological separation between humans, roles, and institutions. Humans are treated as finite biological and cognitive substrates; roles as load-bearing structural constructs; and institutions as mechanical systems of authority, information, and accountability. Building on this foundation, the paper formalizes a sequence of interdependent logic layers that include Faculty Activation Mapping (FAM), structural load and vulnerability diagnostics, dynamic tension analysis, governance attribution logic, and explicit ethical safeguards. Across all layers, measurement is role-level and structural; individuals are never the unit of inference.

The framework introduces diagnostic constructs such as activation levels, load distribution, structural vulnerability indices, and a triage–attribution–prescription decision logic to distinguish design failure, governance failure, stewardship breach, and systemic stress. Crucially, ITS rejects full integration and automation, embedding contestability, auditability, and human judgment as non-negotiable governance constraints.

This paper is conceptual in nature. It does not claim empirical validation, nor does it propose an operational assessment system. Instead, it establishes a disciplined architectural foundation for subsequent research on measurement without psychometrics, burnout as structural exhaustion, ethical accountability, and institutional resilience. By repositioning talent as a problem of structural intelligence rather than individual optimization, ITS offers a rigorous alternative to prevailing paradigms and a defensible basis for sustainable institutional design.

detail.abstract: The authors propose a customer-response model that recognizes the evolvement of customer demand for various products, the possible multifaceted roles of cross-selling solicitations for promotion, advertising, and education, and customer heterogeneous preference for communication channels. They formulate cross-selling campaigns as solutions to a stochastic dynamic programming problem in which the firm's goal is to maximize the long-term profit of its existing customers while taking into account the development of customer demand over time and the multistage role of cross-selling promotion. The model yields optimal cross-selling strategies for how to introduce the right product to the right customer at the right time using the right communication channel.

detail.abstract: In recent years, the United Kingdom has witnessed a significant increase in its immigrant population, driven by factors such as globalization, education, and labour mobility. As a result, ethnic food businesses have emerged as cultural and economic bridges between immigrant communities and the wider UK population. These establishments initially catered to people from similar ethnic backgrounds, but they are now more well-liked by local and multicultural customers who are keen to try out different culinary customs. Nonetheless, many ethnic eateries aim to draw in a sizable clientele and frequently modify their original dishes to accommodate regional preferences and standards. Although this strategy can increase business success, it frequently causes conflicts regarding the offered cuisine's legitimacy. Some customers seek genuine, unaltered flavours that reflect the original cultural heritage, while others prefer modified versions that align more closely with familiar tastes. This makes it difficult for managers or owners of ethnic restaurants to attract diverse types of clients in the UK while simultaneously preserving the culture and maintaining authenticity. Therefore, by surveying both customers and managers points of view, this dissertation seeks to explore the function of ethnic food businesses in the UK and ascertain whether authenticity is important for a business to flourish, utilising primary and secondary data analysis.

title: Consumer Adaptation to a Currency Reform: Illicit Cash Use and Digital Payments
affiliations: Mitchell E. Daniels, Jr School of Business, Purdue University, Yale School of Management and

detail.title: Consumer Adaptation to a Currency Reform: Illicit Cash Use and Digital Payments
detail.abstract: We examine consumer adaptation in payment use to a major currency reform, using India's 2016 demonetization as a natural experiment. Currency reforms that abruptly withdraw or redesign legal tender aim to curb unaccounted cash and promote digital payments, but they can also trigger hidden, illegal adaptation. India's reform, which invalidated 86% of circulating currency, created both a temporary shortage of legal tender and an urgent need for consumers to dispose of banned notes. Using detailed customer-level transaction data from a leading e-commerce platform and cross-regional variation in corruption, we apply a forensic economics approach to detect illicit use of demonetized cash in cash-on-delivery (COD) transactions, by colluding with corruptible delivery-agents. We do so by leveraging three sequential stages of customers' purchase journey: order placement, acceptance at delivery, and returns after acceptance. We find consistent evidence of illicit cash conversion, including an increase in the use of COD for high-price items, a higher acceptance rate of COD transactions in more corrupt regions, and a higher average return rate in COD transactions, during the 50-day conversion window. A latent-class analysis shows substantial heterogeneity: roughly half of customers adopted or increased digital payment use, while about a quarter circumvented the reform using illicit cash via COD. Thus, although the currency reform spurred digital adoption, its effectiveness in curbing unaccounted cash was weakened by illicit consumer adaptation.

detail.title: The Squeaky Wheel Gets the Grease — An Empirical Analysis of Customer Voice and Firm Intervention on Twitter
detail.abstract: This paper investigates customers’ compliments and complaints and firms’ service interventions on social media. We develop a dynamic choice model that explicitly accounts for the evolutions of both customers’ voicing decisions and their relationships with the firm. Voices are driven by both the customers’ underlying relationships and other factors such as redress seeking. The model is estimated using a unique data set of customer voices and service interventions on Twitter. Our findings indicate that redress seeking is a major driver of customer complaints. Although service intervention improves relationships, it also encourages more complaints later, creating a dynamic tension for firms managing social media engagement.

detail.abstract: This paper examines purchases of extended service contracts, which are essentially insurance products, for electronic products in a retail setting. The primary insurance purchase determinants are perceived probability of loss, extent of loss, risk aversion, and amount of insurance premium. The study examines how product characteristics (hedonic/utilitarian nature, manufacturer’s warranty length) and retailer actions (promotions, feature advertising) influence the purchase of extended service contracts. Drawing on surveys of 604 households analyzing electronics purchases, the findings show that just under one-third of consumers bought extended contracts, with purchase decisions driven by product type, perceived risk, and retailer promotional activity.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural model of household behavior in an environment where there is uncertainty about brand attributes and both prices and advertising signal brand quality. Four quality-signaling mechanisms are at work: (1) price signals quality, (2) advertising frequency signals quality, (3) advertising content provides direct (but noisy) information about quality, and (4) use experience provides direct (but noisy) information about quality. The model is estimated using scanner panel data on ketchup. The results imply that price is an important quality-signaling mechanism and that frequent price cuts can have significant adverse effects on brand equity.

detail.abstract: We estimate the causal effect of a sustained electricity blackout on hospital admissions and birth outcomes, exploiting the November 2020 Amapá crisis as a quasi-natural experiment. A lightning-induced fire at the Macapá 230 kV substation — whose backup transformer had been offline for eleven months, leaving zero N-1 redundancy — triggered a 22-day blackout affecting 750,000 residents of Brazil's most grid-isolated state. Two-way fixed-effects DiD on 5,572 municipalities finds a +14.8% increase in hospital admissions (p = 0.023), rising to +23.4% when the COVID second-wave overlap is excluded and validated by a synthetic control showing a -12.7% consumption gap. ICD-10 decomposition reveals three mechanisms: infectious disease admissions +103% (refrigeration/water failure), endocrine/metabolic +24% (insulin cold-chain), and circulatory +12% (powered-equipment loss). SINASC birth records document reduced cesarean capacity, deteriorating Apgar scores, and elevated preterm rates, grounding the case for mandatory redundancy standards in isolated grid systems.

detail.abstract: This white paper evaluates the condition, performance, and economic consequences of deferred investment in U.S. roads and bridges and presents engineering and policy strategies for sustained improvement. Using national performance indicators and recent infrastructure report-card findings, it connects roadway deterioration, bridge aging, congestion, and reliability degradation to measurable household costs, freight inefficiency, and public safety exposure. The analysis considers how funding mechanisms, particularly fuel-tax-based revenue models, have lagged infrastructure needs and how that mismatch contributes to maintenance backlogs and uneven state-of-good-repair outcomes. It then assesses how recent federal policy, including the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, has expanded funding for bridge repair, safety, and resilience while emphasizing performance management and accountability. The paper concludes with a technical roadmap focused on lifecycle asset management, targeted bottleneck elimination, safety-by-design countermeasures, climate adaptation for pavements and structures, and sustainable financing strategies to maintain a consistent state of good repair under rising travel demand.

detail.title: An Empirical Analysis of Consumer Purchase Decisions Under Bucket-Based Price Discrimination
detail.abstract: Bucket-based price discrimination is a unique price format that involves monthly subscription fees and instantaneous quotas (the number of rental products that can be checked out). The authors propose an empirical model in which consumers make dynamic purchase decisions under consumption uncertainty, accounting for the constraints imposed by the instantaneous quota. Applying the model to an online DVD rental data set, the findings show that consumers incur a large disutility from stockout (unmet consumption needs), which drives consumers' overpurchase of the service quota as a way to avoid potential stockout situations. The dynamics of overpurchase are driven by the interplay between trends in consumption needs and the magnitude of consumers' plan-switching costs.

title: Don't Mix What Should Be Separated: Why Combining Value and Momentum Signals Destroys Alpha

detail.title: Don't Mix What Should Be Separated: Why Combining Value and Momentum Signals Destroys Alpha
detail.abstract: Factor investing has established itself as a foundational framework in modern portfolio management, offering systematic exposure to well-documented sources of excess returns while mitigating the behavioral biases that often impair discretionary decision-making. Among the most extensively studied factor combinations is the pairing of value and momentum, whose well-documented negative correlation provides substantial diversification benefits. However, while the merits of combining these two factors are broadly recognized, the existing literature has devoted comparatively limited attention to the specific methodology by which such combination should be implemented. This paper addresses this gap by conducting a rigorous empirical comparison of two predominant approaches: the combined ranking method, which integrates value and momentum signals into a single composite scoring system, and the separate sleeves method, which maintains independent value and momentum long/short portfolios within a multi-strategy book. Using the Top 1,000 U.S. equities over the period 2000–2026, with long/short dollar-neutral portfolios, monthly rebalancing, and 100 positions per side, the study finds that the separate sleeves approach delivers superior risk-adjusted performance. While the combined ranking method produces a higher annualized return (3.01% versus 2.73%), the separate sleeves approach achieves a higher Sharpe ratio (0.168 versus 0.157) with substantially lower volatility (5.51% versus 7.71%) and a markedly shallower maximum drawdown (−17.48% versus −26.61%). A volatility-matched comparison confirms that the separate sleeves methodology outperforms by 52 basis points annualized when both strategies are equalized at the same risk level. These results are attributable to the separate sleeves framework's preservation of the negative correlation between value and momentum return streams (−0.349), which functions as an organic diversification mechanism that is structurally diluted under the combined ranking approach. The paper concludes by discussing practical implementation considerations, including the increased trading intensity and position count inherent to the separate sleeves method, the tail risks associated with shorting momentum losers, and the need for further validation across international markets.

detail.abstract:
Institutional credit investing synthesizes heterogeneous information—financial performance, legal structure, market signals, and forward-looking risk—under time constraints and uncertainty. Traditional credit workflows remain document-centric and episodic, potentially limiting consistency and early detection of deterioration. Recent advances in retrieval-grounded language models and structured reasoning systems suggest the potential to augment analyst judgment through continuously updated decision support, though significant implementation and validation challenges remain.

This paper presents a conceptual framework for AI-enabled Credit Intelligence Systems (CIS) grounded in institutional credit practices. The contribution is a modular architecture, lifecycle mapping, and governance framework designed to address information fragmentation and provide portfolio-aware decision support while preserving human ownership of investment decisions. We discuss implementation considerations, model risk controls, and realistic use cases, while acknowledging that empirical validation of such systems remains an open research question.

title: Are Consumer Demand Models in Developing Countries Biased When they Ignore Farm Profit Effects? Evidence from Malawi
affiliations: , University of Georgia and University of Georgia

detail.title: Are Consumer Demand Models in Developing Countries Biased When they Ignore Farm Profit Effects? Evidence from Malawi
detail.abstract: We estimate household demand for maize, pulses and nuts, and fruits and vegetables using an Exact Affine Stone Index (EASI) framework to quantify how ignoring the "profit effect"-the additional income producers receive when staple prices rise-can bias demand estimates in Malawi. We compare three specifications: a standard EASI with a net-maize-seller shifter; a fully interacted EASI (FI-EASI) that allows price and expenditure elasticities to vary by household type; and an agricultural household EASI (Ag-EASI), our proposed model, that endogenizes real total expenditure so that maize price changes can shift household income and, in turn, demand. We find that across models, food demand is strongly responsive to total expenditure, but Ag-EASI often overturns the conclusions of EASI / FI-EASI. Own-and crossprice elasticities also differ in important ways under Ag-EASI, with shifts in magnitude and, at times, sign. We explore the policy implications by simulating a 10% maize price increase on demand. Results suggest that, whereas EASI/FI-EASI attribute impacts to substitution and income, Ag-EASI's added profit channel reshapes the decomposition and, in some cases, the sign or magnitude. The results suggest that policy instruments may be misguided if they treat all households as pure consumers and ignore producer income responses to staple price changes in a developing country setting.

title: Synergistic Effects of Reputation and Q-Learning on Cooperation in the Prisoner’s Dilemma with an Extortion Strategy
affiliations: Zhejiang University of Finance and Economics (ZUFE), Zhejiang University of Finance and Economics (ZUFE), Nanyang Technological University, University of Science and Technology of China, Zhejiang University of Water Resources and Electric Power and Zhejiang University of Water Resources and Electric Power

detail.title: Synergistic Effects of Reputation and Q-Learning on Cooperation in the Prisoner’s Dilemma with an Extortion Strategy
detail.abstract: Cooperation, a cornerstone of natural and human systems, remains a complex phenomenon whose mechanisms require deeper exploration. A reputation-driven extension of the Prisoners Dilemma was introduced in this study, integrated wit the Q-learning algorithm, to examine how reputation mechanisms interact with extortion strategies in promoting cooperation. By incorporating zero-determinant strategies, notably extortion, cooperation and defection, we simulate strategic evolution on a structured population. Here, the evolution of cooperation is governed by a critical synergy between individual payoffs and reputation. In this framework, cooperation evolves through a critical synergy between individual payoffs and reputation, transforming the game from a mere payoff-optimization task into a dynamic socio-ecological system where agents continuously weigh economic gains against social standing. Our results demonstrated that although reputation mechanisms exhibit hysteresis and require time to accumulate, they ultimately suppress defection effectively. Rational agents prioritize payoff maximization only after surpassing a reputation threshold. Consequently, misaligned incentives can trap the population in a socially inefficient equilibrium characterized by non-negative reputations yet low payoffs. However, realigning incentives within a reasonable range could resolve this dilemma, prompting consistent cooperation. Well-structured payoff incentives thus harmonize individual and collective rationality, leading to high-payoff, high- reputation outcomes.

title: When Women make a Difference: A Natural Experiment on the Globalization Effects of Gender Quotas

detail.title: When Women make a Difference: A Natural Experiment on the Globalization Effects of Gender Quotas

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This study uncovers novel findings on how electoral gender quotas causally shape the national level of globalization. Applying a rich set of empirical strategies that exploit staggered policy intervention across 163 countries from 1980 to 2022, the analysis shows that national legislative gender quotas lead to significantly 0.6-1.4 point increases in the national level of globalization at both adoption and implementation phases. Importantly, the gains from globalization are driven almost entirely by legislated candidate quotas, whereas reserved-seat quotas show little evidence of effect. Moreover, the impact of gender quotas is concentrated in de facto rather than de jure globalization and operates primarily through the social dimension of globalization, with limited responses in economic and political components. Besides, to shed light on the shifts in social norms and institutional practices, the study further confirms potential mechanisms, including increased women's parliamentary representation and improvements in women's social equity and personal autonomy rights, rather than changes in women's economic participation rights. Collectively, these findings freshly explore the globalization effects of gender quota policy that extend beyond descriptive political inclusion, thereby opening new avenues for institutional design and reform.

title: Intention Inference, Greenwashing, and Asset Prices
affiliations: University of Calgary - Haskayne School of Business

detail.title: Intention Inference, Greenwashing, and Asset Prices
detail.abstract: Investors evaluating sustainability disclosures face a fundamental intention-inference problem: do observed climate actions reflect genuine climate commitment or strategic image management? We develop a Bayesian model in which investors form beliefs about managerial sincerity from prior climate-related communication and update these beliefs upon observing subsequent climate actions. The model predicts that identical climate actions generate different market reactions depending on inferred intent, with misclassification of strategic actions as sincere leading to temporary mispricing followed by correction. To test these predictions, we construct a firm-level measure of inferred managerial intent based on the specificity, cross-venue consistency, and forward-looking orientation of climate-related communications in the twelve months preceding each announcement. Using a sample of 4,812 climate-related corporate actions by U.S. publicly traded firms from 2005 to 2023, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in inferred sincerity is associated with a 1.28-percentage-point larger three-day cumulative abnormal return around subsequent climate announcements, after controlling for firm characteristics, climate performance, and action type. We further document that the intention-inference signal predicts cross-sectional stock returns. A long-short portfolio sorted on the joint signal of action strength and inferred sincerity earns a monthly alpha of 0.42% (CAPM) and 0.31% (four-factor model). Long-horizon panel regressions also reveal a reversal among low-sincerity firms that is difficult to reconcile with standard risk-based explanations. These findings identify investor intention inference as a key determinant of the pricing of climate disclosures, a distinct channel through which imperfect attribution of managerial credibility generates predictable mispricing and return dynamics beyond what realized climate performance can explain.

detail.abstract: This article explores various understandings of anti-discrimination law and how different national apex courts, regional human rights tribunals and international human rights treaty bodies have applied them in abortion decisions, particularly in the Global South.  Recent jurisprudential and theoretical innovations in anti-discrimination law range from direct discriminatory treatment against individuals to indirect discrimination resulting in disparate impact on groups to systemic forms of discrimination that address underlying gender hierarchies and prejudicial constructions of women, girls and pregnant persons. Whatever form of anti-discrimination law is applied, they all have a role in improving access to essential abortion services and improving the equal exercise of autonomy. The article proceeds by exploring how courts have reasoned or could have reasoned regarding (i) direct discrimination; (ii) various grounds of discrimination and their underlying wrongs; (iii) indirect discrimination; and (iv) systemic discrimination.  The goal of the article is to generate further debate on how anti-discrimination law has been and can be used to strengthen reproductive equality.

detail.abstract:
This chapter examines the two central copyright questions raised by artificial intelligence: whether AI-generated works can attract copyright protection, and whether training AI models on copyrighted material constitutes infringement. On authorship, it surveys developments across China, the UK, and the United States, finding an emerging consensus that purely autonomous AI outputs are not copyrightable, but works involving sufficient human creative intervention may qualify for protection, positioning generative AI as a tool akin to Photoshop rather than an independent author.

On infringement, the chapter distinguishes between the input phase (copying works into training datasets) and the output phase (models reproducing protected content). It analyses text and data mining exceptions under UK law, the EU's DSM Directive, and US fair use, noting that no jurisdiction has yet reached a definitive resolution. The chapter argues that output litigation may ultimately prove more consequential, raising novel questions about secondary liability and the applicability of intermediary liability frameworks to AI providers. Finally, it examines the copyright-specific provisions of the EU AI Act, including GPAI transparency obligations and the Code of Practice, situating these within the broader effort to balance innovation with the protection of creators' rights.

title: What is the False Discovery Rate in Finance?

detail.title: What is the False Discovery Rate in Finance?
detail.abstract: This seminar shows that the false discovery rate (FDR) in finance is not identifiable from published in-sample statistics unless latent search and selection are modeled explicitly. Once reported factors are viewed as selected outcomes from many tried specifications rather than as single-trial draws, standard mixture-based methods become misspecified and biased, causing the implied FDR to rise sharply. Fitting a search-adjusted model to the cross-section of reported Sharpe ratios yields an estimated FDR above 80%, supporting the view that most published discoveries in finance are false. The implication is that the “factor zoo” should no longer be treated as a reliable map of investment opportunity.

detail.abstract: This study proposes a new approach to predicting corporate bankruptcy by shifting the focus from predicting failure to ensuring firm survival. While existing research largely treats bankruptcy as a symmetric classification problem, we argue that survival and failure are governed by distinct financial mechanisms that require separate analytical approaches. Using a large panel of US firm-year observations from an open-source dataset, we have developed a two-step classification framework that is grounded in internal financial data and working capital dynamics. First, firms that are structurally insulated from bankruptcy are identified based on a strategic credit policy indicator related to the absence of trade receivables. The second step involves evaluating bankruptcy risk among the remaining firms using a parsimonious receivables-to-revenue measure that captures exposure to liquidity constraints. The framework relies exclusively on simple, interpretable accounting ratios and avoids high-dimensional feature sets or opaque algorithmic techniques. Empirical results demonstrate that this sequential approach identifies a significant proportion of firms with a very low risk of bankruptcy, while focusing insolvency prediction on a smaller, financially homogeneous group. By prioritising interpretability and financial logic, the study provides an alternative to the increasingly complex artificial intelligence and machine learning models that are currently in use. The findings emphasise the pivotal role of credit policy and working capital discipline in corporate survival, suggesting that parsimonious, theory-consistent indicators can provide reliable early warning signals over multi-year periods.

detail.title: Foreign Exchange Hedging and Currency Invoicing: Part I Theory
detail.abstract: We study how firms jointly determine currency invoicing and foreign exchange (FX) hedging by incorporating forward contract transactions into a canonical currency-choice framework. We show that (i) in the presence of imperfect hedges and (ii) hedging and pricing decisions are interconnected, FX hedging costs almost always affect currency invoicing. This interaction operates through two distinct channels: First, firms manage exchange-rate risk through two margins-currency invoicing and FX hedging-and hedging costs shape the relative use of these two tools. Second, hedging costs affect firms' hedging positions, which in turn alter exchange-rate pass-through into prices and thereby affect optimal currency choice. Specifically, lower hedging costs in dollars facilitate more effective risk management for firms' dollar exposure, incentivizing them to invoice in dollars-an effect especially pronounced for firms with long dollar positions. Altogether, our results elucidate how dollar dominance in FX transactions reinforces its dominance in trade invoicing, highlighting a fundamental policy tension between the internationalization of domestic currencies and the deepening of FX hedging markets.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the potential paradigm shift from human-machine competition to strategic collaboration in the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI). It examines the "AI Bubble" narrative through the lens of narrative economics, exploring the potential use of risk discourse as an instrument for market positioning and regulatory capture. Integrating the Law of Accelerating Returns and Platform Capitalism theories, this manuscript discusses a conceptual framework for AI Infinity grounded in the philosophical contribution of Futuristic Tauhid (Anggoro, 2025) and the normative principles of Maqasid Syariah. Through an analysis of Market Concentration indicators (HHI) and Capital Intensity models, the paper explores potential institutional designs for an Independent Oversight Board and the necessity of Compute Sovereignty, aiming to seek a global balance via the Zero Polar Equilibrium model based on moral maturity (Anggoro, 2024).

detail.title: Forecast Combination with AI-Generated Narrative States: Bias, Correction, and Inference
detail.abstract: This paper studies forecast combination when the state that drives time-varying weights is estimated from text rather than observed directly. When a generated narrative state enters a nonlinear simplex-constrained weight map, the usual two-step plug-in estimator can fail at first order, distorting both the center and the spread of the limiting distribution. We prove this in a benchmark logistic model, extend the result to a multivariate softmax setting with an explicit Jacobian characterization of the bias, and show that block cross-fitting eliminates the firstorder contamination. In an application using public Federal Reserve communication to reweight competing inflation forecasts, naive rolling-path standard errors are 39 to 291 times smaller than correct sandwich standard errors, producing uniformly spurious significance. Corrected inference reveals that whether narrative states matter depends on the state dimension, forecast pool, and sample period. The main contribution is inferential: it shows that the generated-state problem is empirically consequential, not merely formal.

The laws on surrogacy in Canada, as outlined by the Assisted Human Reproduction Act (AHRA), are a tedious landscape to navigate due to ambiguous reimbursement guidelines. Consequently, reimbursement agreements remain legally unrecognized, allowing for the exploitation of broad reimbursement regulations through disguised forms of compensation. This article attempts to demonstrate the urgent need to amend the legal framework surrounding surrogacy and the potential of enforceable reimbursement to address this gap. In its first part, the article outlines the laws on surrogacy at the federal and provincial levels and demonstrates the shortcomings that undermine the well-being of surrogate mothers, as well as the foundational principles that inform the law. Second, the analysis of peripheral arguments related to enforceable reimbursement occurs, as it evaluates intersecting ethical and legal factors important to the development of new surrogacy-related policies. Lastly, the article discusses the growing concern for the exploitation of surrogates and demonstrates its maintained relevance in the Canadian landscape. Ultimately, this article argues that current laws are unable to meaningfully protect surrogate mothers and highlights the surrogate-oriented, risk-mitigating potential of enforceable reimbursement.

detail.title: Stroke Team Workforce Maldistribution in Indonesia: A Burden-Based Policy Analysis
detail.abstract: BackgroundStroke remains the leading cause of mortality and disability in Indonesia, yet health workforce planning continues to rely largely on population-based norms rather than health need indicators. This misalignment risks exacerbating inequities in access to care across the archipelago.ObjectiveTo examine the alignment between provincial stroke burden and key stroke team workforce availability, and propose a burden-based framework for future workforce planning.MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional analysis across 34 Indonesian provinces. Provincial stroke burden was measured using disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023, mapped against 2025 subnational workforce registry data for neurologists, neurosurgeons, and physiotherapists. Burden-to-workforce ratios were calculated, and provinces classified into high, moderate, or low service pressure categories using a percentile-based approach.ResultsSubstantial interprovincial variation was observed. Eight provinces experienced high service pressure for neurologists, with similar patterns for neurosurgeons and physiotherapists. Although national workforce density met aggregate benchmarks, burden-adjusted analysis revealed significant territorial inequities. Comparative analysis with population-based standards demonstrated that burden-adjusted metrics provide greater sensitivity in identifying priority workforce distribution.ConclusionsA structural mismatch persists between stroke burden and workforce capacity in Indonesia. Integrating burden-based indicators into workforce planning offers a more equitable and epidemiologically responsive framework for allocating specialized health personnel amid the growing non-communicable disease transition.

title: Light-Driven Boosted Uranium Adsorption on Phosphate-Modified MXene Hydrogel for Remediation of Uranium-Bearing Wastewater

detail.title: Light-Driven Boosted Uranium Adsorption on Phosphate-Modified MXene Hydrogel for Remediation of Uranium-Bearing Wastewater
detail.abstract: Nuclear energy expansion drives increasing uranium demand, yet acidic in-situ leaching generates toxic, radioactive wastewater that poses severe ecological and health risks. Conventional treatment methods face efficiency, cost, and operational constraints, necessitating high-performance adsorbents. Here, we report a phosphate-functionalized MXene composite hydrogel (P(AM-VPA)/MXene) synthesized via in-situ polymerization for uranium capture. The material demonstrates exceptional mechanical stability, efficient photothermal conversion, a maximum adsorption capacity of 1396.3 mg·g-1 (Langmuir model) at pH 6, high selectivity for uranium over competing metal ions, and 88.3% capacity retention after six adsorption-desorption cycles. Under visible light irradiation, adsorption efficiency increases by 18.4% due to accelerated ion diffusion. MXene reinforcement optimizes the hydrogel’s porous architecture while providing abundant active sites, synergizing with phosphate groups to enable chemisorption-dominated uranium binding. This work introduces a practical strategy for efficient uranium recovery and environmental remediation, advancing hybrid adsorbent design for radioactive wastewater treatment.

As this ecosystem grows, the need for a standardized framework to assess oper- ational readiness and competency across the spaceflight workforce becomes increasingly important. The Spaceflight Training and Advanced Readiness (STAR) Certification Framework introduces a competency-based professional certification system designed to validate the knowledge, operational skills, and mission readiness of personnel participating in spaceflight missions. STAR defines a structured progression of certifications spanning foundational spaceflight knowledge, spacecraft mission operations, vehicle operations, and human astronaut readiness. By establishing clear competency standards and certification pathways, the STAR framework aims to improve mission safety, operational consistency, and workforce preparedness across the rapidly expanding spaceflight industry.

title: Cognitive Governance: Semantic Infrastructure, Structural Language, and the Pre-Institutional Organization of Power

detail.title: Cognitive Governance: Semantic Infrastructure, Structural Language, and the Pre-Institutional Organization of Power

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework for analyzing a structural transformation in the operation of power in contemporary societies. It argues that power increasingly operates not primarily through institutions, policies, or formal governance mechanisms, but through the organization of cognition itself. Meaning structures, interpretive frameworks, and semantic architectures now precede institutionalization, shaping what can be recognized as rational, legitimate, and governable before formal governance structures emerge. The paper introduces the concept of cognitive governance to describe this transformation: a mode of power that operates by structuring cognition as a governance space. Rather than treating governance as institutional control, the framework theorizes governance as the structural organization of intelligibility itself. Power functions through the stabilization and circulation of cognitive structures that define perception, reasoning, and interpretation prior to institutional formation. By developing the concepts of semantic infrastructure, structural language, and pre-institutional semantic circulation, the paper provides an analytical vocabulary for describing how meaning structures function as infrastructures of governance. It proposes a structural diffusion model in which cognitive architectures circulate through platform-mediated environments, stabilize socially through bypass diffusion pathways, and become institutionalized only after achieving pre-institutional semantic stabilization. The framework integrates and extends core traditions in social theory, including Foucauldian governmentality, Bourdieusian symbolic power, Science and Technology Studies, cognitive sociology, and social constructionism. Rather than offering an empirical case study, the paper develops a conceptual architecture and theoretical model that reposition cognition as a governance space and meaning infrastructures as primary sites of power. By theorizing cognition as a domain of governance, the paper reconfigures the relationship between power, knowledge, and social order. It proposes a structural shift in power analysis from institutions to infrastructures of meaning, from behavioral regulation to cognitive organization, and from institutional authority to semantic intelligibility. The paper concludes by outlining the implications of cognitive governance for social theory, democratic theory, and future research on power in digitally mediated societies.

title: A Legal Analysis of Money Laundering of Proceeds of Corruption in Kenya: A Study of the Role of the Church

detail.title: A Legal Analysis of Money Laundering of Proceeds of Corruption in Kenya: A Study of the Role of the Church
detail.abstract: Over the years, the fight against corruption has intensified across the globe and particularly in Kenya. Corruption in Kenya is a historical problem which the Kenyan government still grapples with to date. The Kenya legislature has over the years enacted laws whose purpose is to aid in curbing the overwhelming problem of corruption in the country. These laws include the Anti-Corruption and Economic Crimes Act (ACECA) and the Proceeds of Crime and Anti-Money Laundering Act (POCAMLA). However, despite these mechanisms put in place by these laws, corrupt officials have devised ways of laundering the proceeds of corruption without detection by law enforcement agencies. This is facilitated by the gaps in the existing laws against corruption and money laundering. Therefore, this paper aims to make a finding on the abuse of religious institutions, churches in particular, in laundering of proceeds of corruption in Kenya as a result of existing gaps in Kenya's anti-corruption and anti-money laundering regimes.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Unruh JD (2001) Postwar land dispute resolution: land tenure and the peace process in Mozambique. International Journal of World Peace. 18: 3-30

detail.abstract: Land tenure issues are fundamentally important to a peace process and agricultural recovery. Disputes over land resources between participants in formal versus customary tenure systems, and the inability of the two to connect in terms of how such disputes are resolved in ways that are viewed as secure and legitimate (and therefore respected) can have especially serious repercussions in periods of recovery from armed conflict. The lack of legitimate adjudication institutions able to resolve disputes between tenure systems has, as the fundamental problem, the existence of evidence relevant to a claim that is available and legitimate within tenure systems, but not between systems. The present work considers the constraints and opportunities for land tenure dispute resolution for groups belonging to customary and migrant tenure systems and formal tenure systems in critical resource (agronomically endowed) areas of postwar Mozambique. From a social survey carried out on 521 households in two provinces of northern Mozambique, the research focused on aspects of postwar customary tenure systems for potential utility as evidence in land dispute resolution within the formal tenure system. Following a brief discussion of the role of land tenure in a peace process, and the land tenure dynamic following civil conflict, the paper looks at critical resources within the landscape of agricultural recovery, and the role of evidence in land dispute resolution. The analysis examines differences between two critical resource areas, and between these and a control, with regard to: evidence type, evidence response to land conflict, and relationships of conflict resolution. The paper ends with look at policy implications.

title: Energy Efficiency, Macroeconomic Shocks, and Housing Market Resilience: Evidence from UK Residential Prices
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Energy Efficiency, Macroeconomic Shocks, and Housing Market Resilience: Evidence from UK Residential Prices
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether energy efficiency affects how UK house prices respond to macroeconomic shocks. While previous research has examined housing price movements and the price premium associated with energy performance, much less is known about how energy efficient homes behave when these economic conditions change. Using transaction level data from England and Wales that links residential sale prices with EPC ratings between 1995 and 2024, we analyse how energy efficiency interacts with key macroeconomic variables, such as interest rates, inflation, and labour market conditions. To allow for nonlinear relationships and interaction effects, we estimate flexible models and use SHAP values to interpret the contribution of macroeconomic and property level factors. Preliminary analysis suggests that properties with higher EPC ratings may be less sensitive to adverse macroeconomic conditions, particularly during periods of rising interest rates. These results suggest that energy efficiency is associated not only with higher house prices, but also with greater price stability, with implications for housing policy and investment decisions.

title: How Monetary Policy Shapes Green Finance: Theory, Mechanisms, and Implications - MENA Region Case

detail.title: How Monetary Policy Shapes Green Finance: Theory, Mechanisms, and Implications - MENA Region Case
detail.abstract: This paper examines how monetary policy affects the allocation of finance between green and brown activities. We develop a macro-finance framework in which green investments are longer-duration and more sensitive to interest-rate changes, while brown activities face higher climate-related transition risk. Using macro-financial and sectoral data for MENA economies, we show that monetary policy is not climateneutral. A 100 basis-point increase in real interest rates reduces green investment almost three times more than brown investment. At the same time, market-neutral balance-sheet expansions disproportionately lower financing costs for carbon-intensive sectors, generating a structural "brown bias." By contrast, credible climate-policy signals significantly reduce green risk premia and increase brown risk premia, leading to a sizable reallocation of capital toward sustainable activities. The results highlight strong interactions between monetary policy, climate transition risk, and financial stability, and underscore the importance of climate-aware monetary and prudential frameworks in carbon-intensive economies.

title: Hierarchical Conditional Memory for Cross-Vocabulary Medical Entity Linking
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Hierarchical Conditional Memory for Cross-Vocabulary Medical Entity Linking
detail.abstract: Objective: To introduce HyCoM (Hierarchical Conditional Memory), a neuro-symbolic framework that decouples static ontology retrieval from dynamic contextual reasoning for extremescale cross-vocabulary medical entity linking, with emphasis on inference efficiency and ontological consistency.Methods: HyCoM integrates three components: (1) a hash-based Conditional Memory module providing 𝑂(1) retrieval over 142,679 UMLS concepts; (2) a Context-Aware Gating mechanism fusing neural query representations with memory-retrieved embeddings; and (3) a two-phase Logic Tensor Network (LTN) training protocol that resolves the cross-entropy/LTN objective conflict by pre-training embedding geometry with LTN-only loss before joint finetuning. Evaluation was conducted on the MedPath-MIMIC-III benchmark (4,486 queries, 142,679 concepts) and the MedMentions ST21pv public benchmark (5,904 in-vocabulary test mentions), with BM25, SBERT+FAISS, and SapBERT+FAISS baselines.Results: On the widely used MedMentions ST21pv benchmark, HyCoM achieves P@1=72.6% and MRR=76.1%, outperforming the SapBERT+FAISS baseline (P@1=63.7%, MRR=70.7%) with high precision. Crucially, the two-phase LTN training protocol successfully resolved underlying structural conflicts, reducing the test Hierarchy Violation Rate from 69.1% to1.2%. To examine cross-domain generalization, we conducted a zero-shot stress test on the MedPath-MIMIC-III dataset. While exact-match metrics were uniformly low across all tested algorithms due to distribution mismatch (synthetic templates vs. real clinical fragments), HyCoM successfully retrieved the target or its hierarchical neighbor (H@5) in 52.3% of cases at 40.1ms CPU latency. Following in-domain MIMIC-III adaptation, H@5 accuracy reached96.77% on the holdout set. Finally, a controlled seen/unseen concept split confirms only a −2.7 percentage point P@1 gap when hash entries are withheld, demonstrating robust generalization to truly novel concepts.Conclusion: HyCoM demonstrates that decoupling memorization from reasoning yields an efficient, hierarchically consistent foundation for medical ontology retrieval. 𝑂(1) hash retrieval scales to vocabulary sizes that challenge FAISS-based dense retrieval, while two-phase LTN training simultaneously achieves high precision and ontological constraint satisfaction.

title: When Renewables Meet Market Power: The Persistence of High Electricity Prices in Italy
affiliations: Università degli Studi di Milano-Bicocca - Center for Interdisciplinary Studies in Economics, Psychology & Social Sciences (CISEPS) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: When Renewables Meet Market Power: The Persistence of High Electricity Prices in Italy
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of renewable energy sources (RES) is expected to exert downward pressureon wholesale electricity prices by increasing the share of low-marginal-cost generation. However,several European markets, notably Italy, continue to exhibit persistently high prices. This paperinvestigates whether strategic bidding behavior in the day-ahead market can explain this apparentdisconnect. We develop a tractable model of multi-unit bidding under uniform-price auctions,allowing for asymmetric firms, heterogeneous technologies, renewable generation, and bilateralcontracting. The model shows that strategic mark-ups are concentrated at the margin and remainsensitive to residual demand conditions, even when a large share of infra-marginal supply isprovided by renewables.We test these predictions using a unique plant-level dataset of bids in the Italian day-aheadmarket over the period 2015–2023. By identifying the most frequently marginal units,we analyzehow their bidding behavior responds to fuel costs, carbon prices, renewable generation, andbilateral contracts. The empirical results indicate that natural gas prices remain the dominantdriver of bids, while the expansion of RES and bilateral contracting has only a limited impacton price formation. Moreover, we find that renewable units, when operating at the margin,exhibit bidding patterns aligned with conventional generators, thereby weakening the expecteddecoupling between electricity and fuel prices.Overall, the findings highlight that renewable deployment alone may be insufficient to ensurecompetitive outcomes. The Italian case provides an informative benchmark, while the analyticalframework is general and applicable to other electricity markets with similar auction structures.

title: Click Wrap Agreements: Valid Consent or Forced Acceptance?

detail.title: Click Wrap Agreements: Valid Consent or Forced Acceptance?
detail.abstract: In the digital age, click-wrap agreements have become an unavoidable part of everyday life, from downloading mobile applications to accessing essential online services. Users routinely click "I agree" without reading or fully understanding the terms, raising an important question: does this click truly represent free and informed consent, or is it simply a compelled acceptance with no real alternative? This paper explores the tension between traditional contract law principles of consent and the realities of digital contracting, where standard-form terms, unequal bargaining power, and time pressures leave users with little meaningful choice. It assesses whether existing legal standards adequately protect user autonomy in online transactions. The paper argues that while click-wrap agreements offer efficiency and certainty in digital commerce, their unquestioned enforcement risks reducing consent to a mere formality. It concludes by emphasising the need for a more context-sensitive legal approach that recognises the lived experience of users while preserving the functionality of digital commerce.

title: Beyond Money, Hedge, and Energy: Evaluating Bitcoin as Power Projection Technology

detail.title: Beyond Money, Hedge, and Energy: Evaluating Bitcoin as Power Projection Technology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author holds Bitcoin. This paper is an academic evaluation of a theoretical framework and does not constitute investment advice.

detail.abstract: In March 2025, the United States established a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve by executive order. Bhutan had been quietly mining Bitcoin with hydroelectric power, accumulating over $1 billion without public announcement. By February 2026, more than 145 publicly traded companies held Bitcoin on their balance sheets, collectively exceeding one million BTC. No established academic framework predicted these developments. In his 2023 MIT thesis Softwar, Major Jason Lowery proposed that Bitcoin is best understood not as money or a hedge but as a power projection technology rooted in thermodynamic proof of work. This paper presents the first empirical evaluation of that framework. Nine falsifiable predictions are tested against observed data; five have been confirmed and one partially realized within three years of publication. The developments that monetary, financial, environmental, and security models fail to explain (strategic reserves, geopolitical competition for hash rate, sovereign mining operations) are precisely those the power projection framework predicts.

title: Three-Layer Civilization Theory: A Systems Model of Capacity, Institutional Efficiency, and Civilizational Outcomes

detail.title: Three-Layer Civilization Theory: A Systems Model of Capacity, Institutional Efficiency, and Civilizational Outcomes

detail.abstract:
Contemporary civilizations face a structural divergence: material capacity continues to grow while biological outcomes—fertility, family stability, and long‑term demographic continuity—sharply decline. Existing frameworks, such as cyclical theories (Toynbee, Spengler), collapse analyses (Tainter, Diamond), and institutional perspectives (North; Acemoglu & Robinson), each illuminate portions of this dynamic but lack a unified mechanism linking resources, institutional efficiency, and biological outcomes within a single analytical structure.

This paper presents the Three‑Layer Civilization Theory, a systems‑engineering model that conceptualizes civilizations through three interacting layers: (1) Capacity (C), representing material, human, and intangible resources; (2) Operating System (OS), representing the institutional transformation mechanism; and (3) Outcome (O), defined explicitly in biological terms as survival and reproduction.

The theory formalizes civilizational dynamics with the input–output equation O = C × η, where η denotes the efficiency of the institutional operating system. A key innovation of the Three‑Layer model is the introduction of a Meta‑Layer—a long‑horizon, partially read‑only subsystem that performs the functions of immunity, stabilization, and reboot. This Meta‑Layer includes enduring cultural lineages, constitutional stabilizers, independent oversight bodies, historical memory mechanisms, and other institutions capable of resisting short‑term volatility.

From this structure emerges a decisive diagnostic rule: If C rises while O falls, institutional efficiency η must be deteriorating. This offers a practical and falsifiable tool for evaluating advanced societies experiencing economic growth alongside demographic decline.

The paper situates the Three‑Layer Theory within existing research, outlines clear falsification tests, and proposes empirical designs using panel data, shock‑response analysis, and institutional decomposition. The Three‑Layer Civilization Theory provides a unified, operationalizable framework for explaining civilizational trajectories and for designing institutions capable of long‑term resilience and demographic sustainability.

The theory yields testable predictions and supports empirical validation through multiplicative model comparison, event‑study shocks, and panel estimation.

title: Battery Storage Cannibalization of Price Spreads in ERCOT

detail.title: Battery Storage Cannibalization of Price Spreads in ERCOT
detail.abstract: Does the rapid buildout of battery storage and solar generation compress intraday electricity price spreads in ERCOT? This paper investigates that question using hourly settlement point prices across five ERCOT hubs from January 2020 through February 2026, combined with monthly installed capacity data. Battery and solar capacity grew in near-lockstep during this period (r = 0.95), making their individual effects difficult to separate in a standard levels regression. The aggregate OLS coefficient on battery capacity is −54 USD/MWh per GW under Newey-West standard errors (p < 0.001); a log specification yields −4.8 percent per GW with R2 = 0.523. Two-stage least squares with month-clustered standard errors produces a first-stage F of 2,228 and γ = −47.75 (p = 0.010). A mechanism decomposition separates the two channels. Batteries significantly compress peak-off-peak spreads (hours 17 to 21 versus 1 to 5, p = 0.04), while solar capacity has no effect on that margin (p = 0.95). Solar instead depresses the midday curve segment. Annualized energy arbitrage revenue fell from 213 USD/kW-yr in 2023 to 61 USD/kW-yr in 2025 as installed capacity grew from approximately 3 GW to roughly 15 GW.

detail.abstract:
This case follows Taylor Ward, a high-performing consultant whose spouse experiences a sudden mental health crisis. As Taylor leads a high-profile client project, they struggle to balance their personal and professional responsibilities. Taylor receives conflicting advice about whether to take personal leave from a results-oriented manager and a more empathetic colleague, highlighting the potential professional costs of stepping back. Meanwhile, Taylor's reduced availability begins to affect their team members, raising questions about the broader impact of their personal issues. Students must consider whether Taylor should take personal leave, which would reduce their pay by 40% until they returned to work, or whether they should continue juggling their personal and professional duties. Students must also evaluate what factors—financial, relational, and professional—should guide that decision.

Excerpt

The Cost of Stepping Back: Taylor Ward's Trade-Offs at Meridian

On a sunny summer day, Taylor Ward hurried through the door of Meridian Strategies (Meridian), a top-tier consulting firm in downtown Boston. Once, Taylor had enjoyed the firm's relentless pace and high expectations, but now, entering the office inspired a rush of dread.

Since joining Meridian two years earlier, Taylor had gained a reputation as a rising star. Composed and reliable, Taylor had successfully executed several time-sensitive projects that had attracted the attention of the firm's senior partners. Several months earlier, Taylor had agreed to lead a new initiative to redesign a major client's operational framework. Although the project required working longer hours, Taylor's manager, Serge Yarov, had implied that it would be a fast track to early promotion.

As the project entered its most critical phase, however, Taylor's spouse, Sam, experienced a sudden and severe mental health crisis requiring intensive support and frequent therapy appointments. Taylor suddenly had to manage medical bills, navigate the couple's insurance coverage, and serve as the primary decision-maker for Sam's care. Stable routines evaporated, replaced by sleepless nights, urgent phone calls, and constant worry. Taylor felt stretched impossibly thin, trying to juggle the domestic load, caring for Sam, and keeping the project on track.

Two Sets of Advice

After a sleepless weekend, Taylor arrived at work on Monday and rushed to their desk to jump into the day. After scanning through the morning's emails, they noticed a message from Serge with the subject line “Come see me immediately.” Taylor's stomach twisted, wondering if they were going to receive bad news about the project. They walked to Serge's office and knocked on the door.

detail.abstract:
Business leaders are under pressure to embrace artificial intelligence (AI) and unlock the benefits that its advocates tout—greater efficiency, reduced headcount, improved experience, increased profitability, and more. At the same time, many voices warn of the potential harmful impacts that AI may have on fairness, the workforce, and society. Still others point out the outsized investment, complex implementation, and difficult-to-realize benefits that make investments in AI an uncertain proposition. These dilemmas require us to think differently about both AI and the ethical considerations that accompany it. The Value Chain of Ethical AI represents a fruitful starting point by equipping us to consider AI as a series of interconnected decisions and actions, each with its own business and ethical implications. The framework provides the roadmap that contemporary leaders need to navigate the complex set of ethical issues that arise along the path to AI-enabled business. Only by considering ethics at each step can we achieve our goal: AI that produces ethical outcomes ethically.This technical note describes the value chain of contemporary AI and introduces some of the ethical and business considerations in each of the chain's five stages. The note is used at the University of Virginia Darden School of Business in the "AI in Government" course for executives. It is also ideal for undergraduate and graduate courses on business ethics, technology, strategy, decision-making, or in any course in which a foundational understanding of the ecosystem supporting contemporary AI applications is necessary.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force across industries, promising unprecedented levels of efficiency, innovation, and productivity. The launch of ChatGPT by OpenAI, Inc. title: Closed-Form Optimal Tontine Payouts under a Discrete-Time Affine Mortality Model
affiliations: University of Western Ontario

detail.title: Closed-Form Optimal Tontine Payouts under a Discrete-Time Affine Mortality Model
detail.abstract: We study the problem of optimal retirement-income design in a pure discrete-time tontine subject to both idiosyncratic and systematic longevity risk. To obtain analytical tractability, we model mortality using a discrete-time affine counting process with a closed-form moment generating function (MGF). This structure allows us to characterize optimal pre-committed CRRA tontine payouts through an exact backward recursion, by linking the MGF to fractional inverse moments of the surviving cohort when risk aversion is low and to integer raw moments when risk aversion is high. We estimate the model by variance-stabilized panel GMM using demographic data from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and the United States, and find evidence consistent with a negative asymmetry in aggregate mortality volatility. We then quantify the welfare implications of stochastic mortality risk through wealth-equivalent-gain (WEG) analysis. Relative to a constant-intensity Gompertz benchmark, stochastic mortality can induce a precautionary reshaping of payouts, lowering early consumption and generating economically meaningful welfare gains, particularly in smaller pools. In our baseline institutional-pool calibration, the resulting closed-form pre-commitment rule is numerically indistinguishable in utility terms from the unconstrained global dynamic-programming benchmark, while remaining substantially more tractable. The results provide a closed-form and empirically calibrated framework for tontine design under stochastic longevity risk.

title: Understanding Gendered Pathways: The Moderating Role of Work-Life Balance in Child Welfare Professionals’ Job Perceptions and Intent to Leave
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh and University of Pittsburgh

detail.title: Understanding Gendered Pathways: The Moderating Role of Work-Life Balance in Child Welfare Professionals’ Job Perceptions and Intent to Leave
detail.abstract: Background: High turnover rates among child welfare professionals have been a consistent issue. While extensive research has identified workplace factors contributing to turnover, the role of work-life balance and its interaction with job perception (including job satisfaction, secondary traumatic stress, and burnout) remains understudied. This study examined how work-life balance moderates the relationship between job perception and intent to leave, and explored whether these dynamics differ by gender and race. Methods: Using Spillover Theory as a framework, this study analyzed data from 830 child welfare professionals in Florida. Gender, education, and years of experience distributions in this sample align with national datasets, though it included a higher proportion of Black participants. Multilevel modeling was used to examine how work-life balance moderates the relationships between job perceptions and intent to leave. Three-way moderation analyses were used to explore whether gender and race influenced these moderations. Results: Work-life balance significantly moderated all three relationships. When work-life balance was high, negative job perceptions had less impact on intent to leave. Notably, consistent gender differences were found. Among females, higher work-life balance reduced the impact of adverse job perceptions on intent to leave, whereas males showed the opposite pattern. These findings suggest females may prioritize work-life balance over job perceptions. Race did not moderate these relationships. Conclusion: Results underscore the importance of organized policies supporting work-life balance, such as flexible schedules and remote work options, while recognizing that strategies must be tailored to workers’ diverse needs and identities rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all approach.

title: Carpal Tunnel Release During Distal Radius Fracture Fixation Is Not Associated with Reduced Subsequent Carpal Tunnel Release: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study
