detail.title: Carpal Tunnel Release During Distal Radius Fracture Fixation Is Not Associated with Reduced Subsequent Carpal Tunnel Release: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study
detail.abstract: Purpose: Prophylactic carpal tunnel release (CTR) during distal radius fracture (DRF) fixation is performed with the goal of preventing symptomatic carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). However, evidence supporting this practice remains limited. This study evaluated whether CTR at the time of DRF open reduction and internal fixation reduces subsequent CTR procedures and other associated surgical complications.Methods: A retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX database identified adult patients who underwent DRF open reduction and internal fixation between 2010 and 2025. Patients were categorized based on whether they received CTR at the time of DRF fixation. Propensity score matching controlled for demographic and clinical variables, including fracture complexity. The primary outcome was subsequent CTR procedure within 2 years. Secondary outcomes included 90-day complications (emergency department visits, readmission, hematoma) and 1-year surgical complications (infection, malunion/nonunion surgery, revision surgery).Results: Among 53,565 patients identified, 5,090 matched pairs were analyzed. Patients who received CTR at the time of DRF fixation did not have significantly different rates of subsequent CTR at 1 year (1.75% vs 1.61%; HR 1.112, 95% CI 0.824-1.501) or 2 years (2.24% vs 1.79%; HR 1.306, 95% CI 0.992-1.721). CTR at the time of DRF fixation was associated with higher rates of revision DRF surgery at both 1 year (2.97% vs 2.10%) and 2 years (3.32% vs 2.36%), malunion/nonunion surgery at both 1 year (0.92% vs 0.53%) and 2 years (0.98% vs 0.63%), and 90-day emergency department visits (7.62% vs 6.03%). Infection rates were not significantly different at 1 year or 2 years.Conclusions: CTR at the time of DRF fixation was not associated with reduced subsequent CTR procedures. These findings do not support routine CTR during DRF fixation.

title: Who Can Afford to Stay Home After Childbirth: Socioeconomic Disparities in the Child Penalty in China
affiliations: Wuhan University and Peking University

detail.title: Who Can Afford to Stay Home After Childbirth: Socioeconomic Disparities in the Child Penalty in China
detail.abstract: Using CFPS data and an event-study design around first births, we document that all mothers experience a sharp decline in labor force participation at childbirth, but postbirth trajectories diverge substantially. Low-socioeconomic-position (SEP) mothers recover their pre-birth participation within four years, whereas high-SEP mothers remain out of the labor force for extended periods. This divergence is explained by the disadvantages faced by low-SEP mothers in terms of financial resources and access to grandparental care. Consequently, low-SEP mothers either incur a double burden when they must juggle work and childcare or suffer from parent-child separation when children are sent to live with non-coresident grandparents. Our study suggests that measurements of child penalty should go beyond pecuniary outcomes and affordable childcare is important for reducing child penalties.

detail.title: Continuing Crisis in Strait of Hormuz: Why Iran's Hold is Illegal and U.S. Military Force Alone Fails

publicationDetails.detailsText: Just Security - Emory Law Research Paper

detail.abstract:
Over a month into the conflict between Israel, Iran, and the United States, Iran has shown no sign of losing its capacity to control the Strait of Hormuz. Although the United States has agreed to a two-week suspension of strikes against Iran, Tehran continues to exercise de facto control over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Foreign Minister has declared that vessels seeking to transit the Strait must coordinate directly with Iranian armed forces, subject to unspecified "technical limitations" -- a posture that amounts to a unilateral assertion of sovereign authority over one of the world's most critical maritime chokepoints. Meanwhile, President Trump has pledged that the United States "will be helping with traffic buildup in the Strait," but that commitment remains undefined, and it is far from certain whether U.S. naval forces will play any role. 

Since the conflict started, Iran has rerouted commercial shipping through Iranian territorial waters and imposed a $2 million transit fee, an illegal "Tehran toll booth." The fragile ceasefire does not appear to dismantle that arrangement. The United States must define the operational scope of its naval commitment in the Strait. And Iran's self-declared "technical limitations" must be rejected outright by the international community and not be made permanent. Limiting transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz is inconsistent with the freedom of navigation guaranteed under international law. At the outset of the conflict, I analyzed the key legal and operational issues in the Strait of Hormuz, assessing that the Strait's closure would provide Iran with enormous strategic leverage. One month in, that assessment has grown considerably darker.

title: Same Underlying, Different Markets: How Convertible Bond Trading Drives Risk Spillovers
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, Capital University of Economics and Business and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Same Underlying, Different Markets: How Convertible Bond Trading Drives Risk Spillovers
detail.abstract: This paper examines how trading in securities with the same underlying asset but different market structures generate risk spillovers. Using intraday high-frequency and order-level data for A-share stocks and convertible bonds in China, we find trading shocks in convertible bonds significantly increase the risk of the corresponding stocks and strengthen intraday tail dependence between convertible bonds and their underlying stocks. Active convertible bond trading does not enhance stock price discovery; instead, it intensifies quantitative and speculative trading in the underlying stocks, particularly for micro-cap and Shenzhen-listed stocks. Risk mitigation measures, such as limiting convertible bond trading to qualified investors or increasing transaction costs to restrain trading frequency, can substantially dampen these spillover effects.

title: Institutional Investor Attention Shift and Insider Trading in Financial Sector
affiliations: California State University Dominguez Hills and Pepperdine University - Pepperdine Graziadio Business School (PGBS)

detail.title: Institutional Investor Attention Shift and Insider Trading in Financial Sector
detail.abstract: We examine whether institutional investor attention shift weakens investor monitoring and creates opportunities for insider sales in financial firms and profit from those sales. Using U.S. financial firms from 2002 to 2019, we measure attention shift with Kempf et al. (2017) portfolio-based institutional investor distraction. We find that greater institutional investor distraction is associated with more intensive insider selling. Distraction is also positively related to higher profitability of opportunistic insider sales measured by buy-and-hold abnormal returns and Fama-French four-factor alphas. The effects are stronger for directors and non-finance officers, under higher quasi-indexer ownership, and around negative earnings surprises. The results from alterative measure of attention shift using Bartik-style instrument on earnings announcement congestion in non-financial industries reaffirm both greater insider selling and greater profitability. We raise concerns that institutional investor attention shift could cause lapses in institutional oversight leading to greater insider sale and profitable opportunistic sale in financial firms.

title: The Negative Beta Pricing Puzzle: A Rational Inattention Solution

detail.title: The Negative Beta Pricing Puzzle: A Rational Inattention Solution
detail.abstract: Recent empirical evidence reveals a striking cross-sectional puzzle: when CAPM beta is decomposed via the covariance network into positive (β +) and negative (β-) components, only β-commands a significant risk premium (Doshi and Jacobs, 2026). This letter provides a parsimonious microfoundation grounded in rational inattention. When investors face a fixed cognitive budget K to process O(N 2) pairwise covariances, the optimal attention allocation follows a water-filling solution. Positive covariances cluster near the default prior and are endogenously ignored (m + ij = 0), whereas negative covariances represent salient deviations that absorb all cognitive resources (m-ij > 0). As N → ∞, the curse of dimensionality forces a strict corner solution that makes the asymmetric pricing of β-versus β + a mathematical necessity, not a behavioral anomaly.

title: Getting To Guardianship: Impacts of Kinship Guardianship Subsidies on Guardianship Permanency for Foster Care-Involved Youth

detail.title: Getting To Guardianship: Impacts of Kinship Guardianship Subsidies on Guardianship Permanency for Foster Care-Involved Youth
detail.abstract: Federal child welfare policies increasingly aim to support kinship guardianship, reflecting evidence that children placed with relatives experience better outcomes. However, estimates on the effects of kinship placement vary considerably by data quality, measurement choices, and approaches to selection bias. This study examines the impact of Title IV-E KinGAP, which offers federal financial assistance to relatives who assume legal guardianship of foster children in their care. Using linked administrative data and exploiting variation in the timing of state KinGAP enactments across the United States from 2009 to 2018, I employ event study methods to examine impacts on exit to guardianship. Results indicate that Title IV-E KinGAP did not significantly influence the likelihood of exiting foster care or exiting to a guardianship placement. These findings suggest that financial support alone may be insufficient to encourage kinship permanency and identifies complementary policy opportunities to more effectively promote kinship placement and permanency for children in foster care.,The Kinship Guardianship Assistance Program (KinGAP) was authorized through the Fostering Connections to Success and Increasing Adoptions Act of 2008 and incentivizes relative guardianship for children in foster care through subsidization with the goal of increasing permanent placement with kin. KinGAP guarantees that children continue receiving financial support once they leave foster care through a kinship guardianship arrangement (HHS, 2021). As of 2021, 37 states and the District of Columbia have enacted Title IV-E federally subsidized guardianship assistance for youth in kinship care. The remaining 13 states did not adopt the Fostering Connections to Success and Increasing Adoptions Act of 2008, but may offer kinship care through expanding state programs, which is controlled for in this study. I use child-level data from national administrative records, state-level child welfare policies, and an original database of effective dates of federally-subsidized Title IV-E KinGAP legislation with quasi-experimental methods to examine the effect of Title IV-E subsidized KinGAP on the probability of exiting to guardianship as a permanency outcome.

detail.abstract:
This is an amicus brief in support of a petition for rehearing (and rehearing en banc) in Syneren Technologies Corp., et al, v. United States (No. 2024-1424). Amici are law professors interested in ensuring that bedrock principles of administrative law, including Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”) standards, are applied to ensure that federal agencies act with integrity, accountability, and engage in fair and regular processes that do not subject contractors to arbitrary and capricious government action.

The brief advocates for U.S. Federal Circuit en banc rehearing on the issue of whether a federal agency can unilaterally, and without leave of the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (“COFC”), change the administrative record during ongoing bid protest litigation over that record. The brief also encourages the Court to revisit unnecessarily broad pronouncements made by the panel as to the inapplicability of foundational principles of administrative law to government procurement decisions. Among other things, the brief discusses the Federal Circuit's embrace of the relevant aspects of Chenery and Regents in bid protest litigation for the important administrative law principle that judicial review of agency action is limited to the grounds that the agency invoked at the time it took the action.

The brief was prepared by Travis Mullaney.

title: The Professionalization Paradox: Why Law-Firm Hiring Unravels

detail.title: The Professionalization Paradox: Why Law-Firm Hiring Unravels
detail.abstract:
Law firms' recruiting timeline has accelerated sharply since the pandemic, with recruitment now moving into the first semester of law school. This acceleration has disrupted legal education, burdened students, and forced firms to make hiring decisions on increasingly limited information. Economists have long recognized this pattern, known as unraveling, as a recurring feature of entry-level professional markets; recent legal commentary has also begun to examine its effects on market participants. Yet these accounts have not fully explained why professional labor markets are especially susceptible to unraveling. As a result, existing responses tend to target surface symptoms of the acceleration without confronting the structural conditions that produce it. 

This Essay offers an institutional account of unraveling in the law-firm hiring market. It argues that pressure toward earlier contracting is an endogenous consequence of law's professionalization. The same historical developments that standardized legal education and organized modern law firms also generated the conditions that make preemptive hiring both feasible and attractive. It then shows why the leading reform strategies are constrained: controlling timing depends on control of the cheapest distribution channel for evaluative signals, while weakening those signals invites firms to substitute their own assessments. Left unchecked, that substitution threatens to displace legal education from the gatekeeping role on which law's professional status depends. Resolving this paradox will require the profession to reconsider the design of legal education so that it can sustain law's claim to professional status while giving employers a reason to wait.

title: The Upside of Unreliability: Screening via Sunk Costs in Platforms

detail.title: The Upside of Unreliability: Screening via Sunk Costs in Platforms

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP21H04979 and JST ERATO Grant Number JPMJER2301, Japan.

detail.abstract: Platforms often require users to incur sunk participation costs (fees, effort, or waiting) before learning whether service will be delivered. We study such environments with a model that separates actual non-delivery risk from perceived risk. When users are naïve about risk, unreliability creates scope for ex post manipulation: within a benchmark class of efficient two-bidder mechanisms, the war-of-attrition (second-price all-pay) format maximizes deviation revenue. When risk is common knowledge but budgets and valuations are misaligned, unreliability instead screens participation. Higher reliability can attract deep-pocket, lower-valuation entrants who crowd out budget-constrained high-valuation users, while intermediate unreliability can induce their exit and may increase consumer surplus discontinuously at the exit threshold. We do not advocate intentional unreliability; rather, we highlight a design tradeoff between trust-enhancing reliability and screening through endogenous entry in settings with unavoidable execution risk and limited commitment.

title: Startup States

detail.title: Startup States

detail.abstract:
This paper advances a treaty-first framework for the lawful creation of new sovereign states within the existing architecture of international law. Departing from unilateral secessionist models, digital “network state” proposals, and extra-legal assertions of sovereignty, the Startup State model proposes a consensual pathway to statehood grounded in formal treaty relations with an existing recognised state.

Drawing upon the Montevideo Convention of 1933, the United Nations Charter, the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, and relevant jurisprudence of the International Court of Justice, the paper examines the doctrinal foundations of statehood, recognition, territorial integrity, and international legal personality. It evaluates both declaratory and constitutive theories of recognition and situates the Startup State model within orthodox principles of sovereign equality and consent-based international ordering.

The paper further contrasts Startup States with micronational movements, special administrative regions, charter cities, and contemporary “network state” proposals, arguing that durable and legitimate sovereignty must arise through lawful agreement rather than technological coordination or unilateral declaration. It proposes that treaty-based sovereign formation offers a peaceful, rules-based mechanism for institutional innovation in governance without destabilising the existing international system.

By reframing sovereignty as a matter of negotiated institutional design rather than revolutionary rupture, this paper contributes to contemporary debates on state formation, recognition doctrine, and the future of political organisation under international law.

detail.abstract: We decompose the total execution cost of trading on decentralized exchanges into visible and hidden components, using 534,198 verified Uniswap v3 swaps from Adams et al. The visible liquidity-provider fee accounts for only 28-36% of total cost; the remainder-gas, adverse slippage, market impact, and maximal extractable value (MEV)-is implicit. We formalize a structural equivalence between MEV and Payment for Order Flow (PFOF): both extract rents from uninformed retail flow via ordering privilege, but MEV provides no offsetting rebate. Exploiting the Merge (September 15, 2022) as a natural experiment, we show that proposer-builder separation increased MEV extraction intensity by eliminating failed-transaction friction. During top-decile volatility, sandwich victimization probability rises approximately 87% for memecoins and adverse slippage quadruples. We estimate cumulative Ethereum MEV exceeds $1.38 billion through mid-2024-comprising $675 million pre-Merge and 526,207 ETH in post-Merge validator revenue-and that sandwich attacks imposed approximately $60 million in cumulative losses over the twelve months ending October 2025, an implicit tax of 2-34 basis points per vulnerable trade depending on asset type, compared with 1-2 basis points under PFOF. These findings argue for encrypted mempools, batch auctions, and regulatory parity between on-chain and off-chain order-flow extraction.

detail.abstract: Despite growing climate-related costs, no standardized metric exists to compare how climate conditions affect household financial pressure across locations. Energy bills respond to extreme temperature days, insurance markets react to wildfire and flood exposure, and health costs rise during heat and air quality events. Yet these cost signals remain scattered across disconnected datasets and hazard indicators, making systematic comparison difficult for households, lenders, insurers, and planners. This paper introduces the Climate Cost Index (CCI), a new composite metric measuring the relative intensity and acceleration of climate-linked cost signals and hazard exposures across U.S. counties, indexed to a national median baseline of 100. It is designed as a standardized measurement framework for comparing climate-linked household cost pressure across locations. CCI integrates two classes of inputs: climate-attributed cost signals, where causal attribution can be identified through regression methodology, and climate-relevant hazard burden proxies, where hazards materially influence household cost pressure but precise climate attribution is not yet separable. The framework preserves this distinction throughout the index. The methodology combines percentile normalization across the national scoring universe, hybrid budget-risk weighting derived from the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey, robust trend acceleration using Theil-Sen slope estimation with denominator protection, and deterministic covariance controls to prevent double counting among correlated hazards. We report the first full implementation across 3,111 U.S. counties. Scores range from 47 to 197 with a median of 106.3, and climate-attributed energy costs average $43 per household annually. Sensitivity testing across eight robustness modules confirms that county rankings remain stable under alternative methodological assumptions. The methodology is fully transparent and replicable using publicly available data.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates how the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which functions as an aggregate statistic, does not show the distributional variation of inflation across the income spectrum. Utilising expenditure-share weights from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Expenditure Survey and category-level price data from the BLS CPI tables, five Laspeyres price indices are constructed for each income quintile, covering the period from January 2019 through December 2024. The data indicate that the lowest-income quintile (Q1) experienced a peak year-over-year inflation rate of 12.44% in June 2022, compared to 10.72% for the highest-income quintile (Q5) and 9.06% for the headline CPI. Cumulatively, Q1 households faced a price level approximately 2 percentage points higher than Q5 households by the end of 2024 relative to a 2019 base. This difference is driven primarily by the higher expenditure shares of lower-income households on food and energy. The paper further tests whether quintile-specific inflation measures improve the prediction of University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment. Headline CPI retains the highest adjusted R 2 of 0.727 in a time-series regression framework. While Q1 inflation and headline CPI Granger-cause sentiment shifts at conventional significance levels, the inflation inequality gap itself does not. These findings carry implications for the communication of monetary policy and the execution of cost-of-living adjustments.

detail.abstract: The rapid scaling of climate and development finance has intensified a central but underexamined challenge: not only how risk is distributed, but how and when it becomes visible. While existing frameworks increasingly acknowledge contingent liabilities, guarantees, and sovereign exposure, they largely assume that risk, once created, can be observed, measured, and governed. In practice, however, risk visibility is neither immediate nor neutral. It is shaped by institutional fragmentation, reporting structures, temporal deferral, and political incentives that systematically delay recognition. This paper argues that the central governance failure is not simply the accumulation of risk, but the absence of mechanisms that render aggregated exposure visible at the point of decision. As a result, what appears manageable at the level of individual instruments becomes binding only once pressures materialize across the system. By shifting the focus from risk allocation to risk visibility, the paper provides a complementary perspective to existing fiscal risk frameworks. It shows that visibility is a precondition for accountability, and that its absence is not accidental but structurally embedded in current approaches to derisking and blended finance. The analysis highlights the implications for policy design, particularly in the context of accelerated investment under energy transition pressures, and outlines the need for governance mechanisms that make exposure visible before it becomes binding.

title: Does Bitcoin's Power Law Deviation Predict Return Distributions? Evidence from the PRESS Model PRESS Model: Power Law Return Sigma Signal

detail.title: Does Bitcoin's Power Law Deviation Predict Return Distributions? Evidence from the PRESS Model PRESS Model: Power Law Return Sigma Signal
detail.abstract: We introduce the PRESS Model (Power Law Return Sigma Signal), a rolling quantile regression conditioned on Bitcoin’s standardised deviation from its power law trend (σ). The model produces a full conditional return distribution at each forecast date — seven quantile forecasts that shift dynamically with σ, enabling both risk assessment and portfolio sizing. Evaluated strictly out-of-sample over 3,135 observations at five forecast horizons, the model outperforms the unconditional benchmark in 34 of 35 quantile-horizon cells, with pinball loss reductions of 4–27%. While the model delivers a statistical edge across the full sample (34 of 35 cells), the information gain is concentrated non-linearly: the most significant tail-risk compression occurs in the 33% of observations where σ exceeds ±1 standard deviation from the trend, with additional upper-tail gains in the moderate zone. The primary specification uses a rolling 4-year quantile regression window, spanning one Bitcoin halving cycle, applied to 5,720 daily observations (July 2010 – March 2026) with an 8.6-year out-of-sample period. The rolling design progressively discards pre-institutional data that could potentially contaminate expanding-window estimates. The model requires only Bitcoin's own price series and updates daily. Log score verification confirms significant distributional information gain (+0.041 nats at h = 14d, p = 0.010, HAC-adjusted). A Half-Kelly BTC/Cash portfolio outperforms buy-and-hold on 100% of 2,771 possible entry dates (≥1-year horizon), reducing the maximum drawdown by 10 percentage points (−73.6% vs −83.8%), increasing the Sharpe ratio to 0.74 from 0.61, and delivering median excess CAGR of +7.8%.

detail.title: The Social Good Shortfall: Reframing Takings Doctrine for Housing-Scarce Cities
detail.abstract: This article argues that takings doctrine in housing-scarce cities should be reoriented around a "social good shortfall" standard. In Hong Kong and other dense urban settings, acute housing shortages coexist with fragmented ownership, underused land, and redevelopment regimes that either defer too readily to economic development or fail to generate meaningful housing supply. Existing formulations of public use, public purpose, and public interest are too open-ended to discipline redevelopment, yet too limited to justify the land assembly needed to address scarcity. The article proposes that compulsory acquisition should be justified only where the current or reasonably foreseeable use of land falls materially short of a feasible alternative in delivering socially important outcomes under conditions of scarcity. Grounded in a modernized reading of Locke's spoilage proviso, the article also develops a framework of "propriety in the taking": a substantial evidentiary basis for acquisition, compensation exceeding bare market value while respecting autonomy, and a decision-making process insulated from capture. It further argues that takings should ordinarily proceed through private-to-private redevelopment subject to independent expert review and judicial scrutiny. Comparative analysis of Hong Kong, the United States, and Seoul shows both the limits of permissive redevelopment and the promise, and trade-offs, of mandatory social housing requirements.

detail.abstract: This paper hypothesizes a flow of information from firms to large shareholders during activist campaigns and its consequences. Focusing on actively managed mutual fund families, we find that informed trading by large-holding fund families increases during activist campaigns relative to smaller-holding fund families invested in the same firms. The effect is stronger for firms that attend more invitation-only investor events, face greater threats from activist campaigns, and are harder to value. Consistent with information flowing from management to large-holding fund families, the effect strengthens when Regulation Fair Disclosure enforcement is lax and when the information is favorable to the firm. Furthermore, the increased information advantage is associated with more management-friendly voting behavior by these investors and a higher likelihood of target firms winning activist campaigns and retaining board seats. Overall, our findings are consistent with a potential quid pro quo in which investors' access to information from management is associated with more pro-management behavior.

title: Brighten-up-DPs: A Guide to Designing and Reporting Rigorous Experimental Dark Patterns Research

detail.title: Brighten-up-DPs: A Guide to Designing and Reporting Rigorous Experimental Dark Patterns Research
detail.abstract: Dark patterns (DPs) are interface designs that exploit users’ cognitive or motivational tendencies and have become central to digital policy debates, yet the empirical foundations of this field remain weak. Most studies describe manipulative features but rarely test whether, why, and for whom they influence behavior. In this article, I highlight key methodological shortcomings in the current experimental DP literature and address them by outlining a practical, theory-driven guide for designing and reporting rigorous experimental research. I argue that cumulative progress depends on explicit theoretical frameworks and falsifiable hypotheses that specify the mechanisms linking interface manipulations to psychological processes and outcomes. Experimental research should aim to explain and predict behavior by aligning empirical findings with behavioral theory and by using validated measurement instruments. I further outline key design considerations for credible causal inference, including randomization and transparent balance checks, appropriate choices between within- and between-subjects designs, control of order effects, clear instructions that minimize demand effects, and incentive-compatible procedures to mitigate hypothetical bias. In addition, I emphasize research quality safeguards such as reliable and valid measurement, attention and awareness checks, transparent sampling and reporting, and justified power analyses. Finally, I stress the importance of preregistering complete research protocols (including all choices and decisions made by researchers) as part of an open science approach that supports replication and policy trustworthiness. These recommendations are integrated into the BRIGHTEN-UP-DPs framework, a comprehensive checklist guiding researchers from theory to transparent reporting. It is my aim to lower barriers to experimentation with this framework, and to strengthen the empirical evidence base on how dark patterns influence users’ perceptions, cognition, emotions, and behavior.

title: A Regulatory Intent Schema for Automated Legal-to-Constraint Translation in Governance-Aware Reinforcement Learning

detail.title: A Regulatory Intent Schema for Automated Legal-to-Constraint Translation in Governance-Aware Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Regulatory compliance in AI systems requires translating natural language legal obligations into formal mathematical constraints. In Governance-Aware Reinforcement Learning (GARL), this translation is performed by the TRANSLATE function-currently a manual, expert-dependent process that does not scale across jurisdictions or regulatory updates. This paper introduces the Regulatory Intent Schema (RIS), a structured intermediate representation that formalizes regulatory provisions into typed, machine-readable objects compatible with the GARL TRANSLATE function. We propose a three-stage hybrid pipeline in which an LLM extracts regulatory intent and populates RIS objects, a rule engine converts RIS objects into formal constraints, and the GARL TRANSLATE function integrates those constraints into the training loop. Case studies across three regulatory frameworks-GDPR, ECOA, and the EU Working Time Directive demonstrate cross-jurisdictional applicability and auditability. RIS provides a practical approach to constraint derivation within the GARL framework, supporting more systematic and auditable legal-to-constraint translation across regulatory domains.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a forward-looking portfolio construction framework that replaces historical covariance with supply chain topology as the basis for risk modeling and alpha generation. We present evidence that the AI-driven transformation of the global economy is producing two approximately orthogonal economic regimes: the Physical Scarcity Graph, encompassing semiconductor fabrication, energy infrastructure, and rare material supply chains; and the Cognitive Abundance Void, encompassing knowledge-work software, professional services, and information intermediaries whose total addressable markets are being absorbed by general-purpose artificial intelligence. Through eigendecomposition of a bidirectional Leontief dependency matrix constructed from observable and estimated supply chain data, we show in calibrated prototype tests that these two regimes occupy approximately orthogonal structural spaces connected only by a thin causal coupling: the rate of AI adoption simultaneously drives demand for physical infrastructure and erodes demand for cognitive-output businesses. This finding challenges the assumption underlying most AI-themed long-short strategies that physical beneficiaries and cognitive casualties are structurally anti-correlated. We formalize a three-layer quantitative system: (1) a Structural Correlation Matrix derived from Tanimoto similarity on a bidirectional dependency graph, producing a naturally positive semi-definite risk model with no eigenvalue correction required-a property we establish via a formal theorem on unified graph similarity metrics; (2) a Scarcity Migration Index that captures the macro causal factor bridging the two regimes, with asset-level Scarcity Betas derived from a combination of observable financial data and estimated structural parameters; and (3) a portfolio optimizer that maximizes alpha per unit of structural risk subject to a scarcity-neutral constraint. Singular value decomposition of the dependency matrix in our calibrated prototype network reveals that a single structural factor-the Scarcity Migration axis-captures 99.9% of total structural variance, with a spectral gap ratio of 32.9:1 over the next largest component. This paper develops the asset-pricing layer of the Scarcity Migration research program; companion papers extend the framework to institutional form (Lambert, 2026b) and operational architecture (Lambert, 2026c).

detail.abstract: The first three papers in the Scarcity Migration series formalize asset pricing (Lambert, 2026a), institutional design (Lambert, 2026b), and operational architecture (Lambert, 2026c) under conditions of cognitive abundance and physical scarcity. All three treat the physical dependency graph as the fundamental analytical object. None model the financing layer that determines whether structural scarcity translates into actual capital formation. This paper identifies and formalizes the missing transmission layer. We introduce a Financing Accessibility Matrix that encodes how regulatory capital treatment, risk-weighted asset classifications, and credit market structure determine whether capital can flow to the nodes where the physical dependency graph demands it. The financing constraint is integrated directly into the adjacency matrix before computing the Leontief inverse, producing a Financing-Constrained Total Dependency Matrix that propagates financing bottlenecks through the same cascade mechanics the SM-APM uses for physical dependencies. We present evidence of the financing-structural wedge across four domains of the physical scarcity graph: industrial equipment (drawing on Rayburn, 2026), data center infrastructure, energy generation for AI compute, and semiconductor capital equipment. The strongest numerical case is industrial equipment, where precise financing cost comparisons are available; the other three domains exhibit the same directional pattern and are presented as motivated cases for further calibration. In each domain, regulatory capital treatment calibrated to pre-AI scarcity conditions appears to underfinance assets whose structural importance is rising. We propose a new axiom system-the Financing Axioms F1-F5-that extends the SM-APM's Structural Axioms to incorporate this constraint, derive a Regulatory Scarcity Distortion measure that quantifies the wedge for each node, and propose instrument architectures that emerge from the dual-graph framework.

title: The Transition to Mandated Ternary Architectures via Memristive Hysteresis

detail.title: The Transition to Mandated Ternary Architectures via Memristive Hysteresis
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the architectural and economic feasibility of transitioning from dominant binary CMOS computing to a "Mandated Ternary" paradigm. The proposed system is defined by a physically stable, non-volatile third logic state ("Null" or "Balance") engineered into memristive devices via hysteresis. This third state is not a software convention but a hardware-enforced checkpoint that gates computational actions, providing a novel mechanism for safety, security, and auditability. The central thesis is that this paradigm offers a discontinuous advantage over incremental binary scaling by directly mitigating the most pressing bottlenecks in advanced semiconductor nodes: interconnect delay, the memory wall, and power density. We provide rigorous analysis of device physics, focusing on Tantalum Oxide (TaOx) RRAM as a primary example. Our analysis quantifies a substantial "emulation tax"-over 15x in energy and 5x in latency-incurred when simulating ternary logic on binary hardware, thereby motivating native implementations. We argue that the rise of agentic AI, with its need for verifiable, enforceable hesitation, serves as a critical catalyst for this architectural shift. The paper concludes with a roadmap to 2027 for achieving industry-standard viability. The key innovation is the concept of Hardware-Enforced Hesitation-a physically unbypassable third state that enables auditable safety mechanisms for autonomous systems.

reference: INSEAD Working Paper No. 2026/21/EPS
title: On Penalties and Premiums: The Impact of Childbirth on the Well-Being and Work of Parents
affiliations: and INSEAD

detail.title: On Penalties and Premiums: The Impact of Childbirth on the Well-Being and Work of Parents

publicationDetails.journalName: INSEAD Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Mitigating gender inequalities in the workplace that arise from parenthood is a key concern of organizations. Research on these inequalities has focused mainly on career and economic and inequalities, yet their effects on well-being, a key dimension of organizational performance, remain largely unexplored. To examine how changes in parents' work outcomes following childbirth affect wellbeing, we use the Understanding Society dataset to track their daily emotions and life satisfaction. We document striking gender differences in how well-being evolves after childbirth. While fathers report persistently lower well-being, the well-being of mothers depends on post-birth career trajectories: those who earn more or return to work full-time experience increased unhappiness, whereas those who reduce their hours or experience wage penalties do not. After showing that these changes reflect parents' increasing dissatisfaction with their work, we discuss how the inflexible nature of many organizations likely contributes to fathers' difficulty balancing family responsibilities with workplace demands and to the trade-off mothers face between career progression and wellbeing. The results of our paper suggest that mitigating gender inequality requires a broader perspective than the conventional focus on economic and career outcomes. Addressing persistent well-being trade-offs faced by working parents may therefore be critical for organizations seeking to retain talent, improve productivity, and maintain long-term performance.

reference: Georgetown University Law Center Research Paper (forthcoming); The Journal of Corporation Law, Vol. 10, pp. 431–462 (1985)
title: Race for the Bottom v. Climb to the Top: The ALI Project and Uniformity in Corporate Law
affiliations: and George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: Race for the Bottom v. Climb to the Top: The ALI Project and Uniformity in Corporate Law

keywords: Principles of Corporate Governance and Structure

publicationDetails.detailsText: Georgetown University Law Center Research Paper (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: Georgetown University Law Center Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Journal of Corporation Law, Vol. 10, pp. 431–462 (1985)

detail.abstract:
The American Law Institute’s (ALl) proposed Principles of Corporate Governance and Structure: Restatement and Recommendations has generated a considerable amount of controversy. A fundamental disagreement between those advocating reform (corporate reformers) and the defenders of the status quo (corporate federalists) about the efficacy of market forces in assuring managerial accountability to shareholders lies at the heart of the corporate governance debate. Corporate federalists argue that various competitive market forces generate incentive structures which force managers toward shareholder wealth maximizing strategies. From this perspective, only minimal government intrusion into internal corporate affairs is deemed proper. Corporate reformers, on the other hand, argue that market forces are ineffective in controlling managerial discretion, and thus a more explicit governmental role is necessary. These conflicting views are most evident in the antagonist’s differing attitudes toward Delaware’s success in the competition between states for the lucrative corporate chartering business. Reformers have labeled the competition as a “race for the bottom,” which refers to Delaware’s allegedly low standards of managerial conduct. Some corporate federalists, on the other hand, prefer to call the competition a “climb to the top,” which refers to the allegedly beneficial attributes of Delaware law in terms of economic efficiency.

This Article suggests that it is not correct to view individual corporation laws as either good or bad. Laws that are good for some firms will be bad for others. That is, it is suggested that mandatory changes in state corporation laws may injure most firms and shareholders while benefiting few others. This Article presents a new theoretical perspective and supportive empirical results. 

The discussion is divided into four parts. The history and current status of the corporate governance debate are discussed in section II. The section begins with a summary of current writings regarding the nature of the corporate agency problem. Section II discusses the alleged harmful effects of competition between the states for the lucrative corporate chartering business, as well as proposals for reforming the current system.

Although reform advocates accept the legal model and corporate federalists accept the market model, the analysis presented in section III suggests that neither position is universally appropriate. Instead, section III proposes a tradeoff model of corporate governance, in which the appropriateness of specific types of corporate governance mechanisms is dependent upon the particular circumstances of individual firms. Discussion then focuses on the marginal (incremental) substitutability of a variety of different corporate governance mechanisms that may be used to fashion an individual firm’s governance structure.

In section IV, the trade-off framework for evaluating corporate governance mechanisms is applied to the analysis of a firm’s selection of its chartering state. Specifically, the relationships between the variable contours of corporate law across state jurisdictions, and the financial performance of corporate organizations are considered. If one corporate law is universally “better” than another, then firms incorporating in that state would appear to have a comparative advantage over firms chartered in other states. However, since we observe successful firms chartered in both strict and liberal jurisdictions, it appears that no one pattern of legal rules and market constraints is uniformly appropriate. That is, corporate governance practices are contingent upon particular corporate circumstances. Thus, calls for uniformity across states in various aspects of corporate law, as implied by the ALI, or a federal incorporation law, as suggested by some commentators, would not necessarily result in increased shareholders’ welfare, which is their putative goal. The shareholder’s welfare appears to be served best by allowing the choice between a variety of corporate laws, any one of which may be optimal under certain circumstances.

A final section summarizes this Article’s major contributions and offers some implications for public policy. Interestingly, while the theoretical and empirical results presented support the reformers’ position that the strictness of fiduciary duties is important to the effective governance of the corporation, they are also consistent with the corporate federalists’ position that the market will force the adoption of governance mechanisms that increase shareholders’ wealth. The major policy implication, however, is consistent with the corporate federalists’ position against centralization and legal activism.

title: No Place Like Home: Understanding Expatriate Behavior in Times of External Threat
affiliations: Hitotsubashi University

detail.title: No Place Like Home: Understanding Expatriate Behavior in Times of External Threat

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: All respondents gave explicit consent and reviewed the final draft before publication.
declarations.funderStatement: The collection of primary data was made possible by funding from the Scholarship Foundation for Studies of Japanese Society.

detail.abstract: Reactions and responses of expatriates in the Tokyo area to the 2011 Tohoku disaster and its aftermath were highly varied, ranging from business as usual to overseas evacuation. In this study, 12 expatriates who lived and worked in Tokyo at the time of the disaster were interviewed face-to-face and the findings analyzed through the lens of expatriate types, crosscultural adjustment and social attachment theory in order to find explanations for their different choices. Results indicate that expatriates relate to a variety of stakeholders-all with different push-and-pull factors-when responding to increased levels of external threat and making evacuation decisions. For well-adjusted expatriates, these stakeholder maps grow in complexity and importance to the expatriate, reducing the likelihood of evacuation. While this is a case study on a single and in many ways unique event, the insights gained could be used in further research on the increasingly important area of expatriate behavior or by organizations when formulating global human resource strategies and emergency preparedness plans.

title: When Does Agricultural Price Volatility Matter for Financial Inclusion? Environmental Constraints and Heterogeneous Effects Across Indian Districts

detail.title: When Does Agricultural Price Volatility Matter for Financial Inclusion? Environmental Constraints and Heterogeneous Effects Across Indian Districts
detail.abstract: Financial inclusion plays a central role in shaping household resilience to economic shocks, yet its relationship with agricultural price volatility remains empirically ambiguous. This paper examines how agricultural price volatility is associated with district-level financial inclusion in India, and whether this relationship varies across environmental contexts. Using a newly constructed district-level price volatility index combined with data on digital payments, economic activity, microfinance penetration, human capital, household welfare, and groundwater stress, the analysis proceeds in two stages. First, a sequence of ordinary least squares models estimates average associations between price volatility and financial inclusion. Second, interpretable machine learning methods, including Random Forests, SHAP decomposition, and causal forests, are employed to uncover nonlinearities and distributional heterogeneity that linear models may obscure. The results show that price volatility does not exert a robust average effect on financial inclusion once structural factors are controlled for. However, substantial heterogeneity emerges across groundwater stress regimes: volatility effects become economically meaningful in groundwater-constrained districts, while remaining weak or highly variable elsewhere. These findings highlight the importance of environmental constraints in conditioning financial inclusion outcomes and demonstrate the value of combining econometric and machine learning approaches to move beyond average effects in development research.

title: How Disasters Drive Action: Subsidiaries, Supply Chains, and Climate Lobbying
affiliations: University of Michigan and New York University (NYU)

detail.title: How Disasters Drive Action: Subsidiaries, Supply Chains, and Climate Lobbying
detail.abstract: Climate change imposes costs on firms that are often difficult to estimate, while corporate climate action generates benefits that are non-rivalrous and non-excludable. This dynamic increases firms' incentives to free ride. Yet, corporate climate lobbying has risen generally across sectors. We develop a theoretical framework where disasters update firms' perception of future costs, motivating present-day action. Ownership and production networks amplify this effect by making costs attributable, measurable, and concentrated, while supplier substitutability hinders corporate climate action. Using a comprehensive dataset linking U.S. firms, domestic subsidiaries, and supply chain partners to environmental lobbying, we find that disasters affecting firms or their subsidiaries increase lobbying, while disasters impacting suppliers matter only when alternatives are scarce. We provide additional evidence that affected firms change their climate risk perception and lobby more on "pro-climate" and "narrow" bills. These results highlight how spatial and structural factors drive climate action in multi-unit, networked firms.

title: A "Useless" Asset Class: Is Kashkari's Skepticism Toward Cryptocurrency Justified?
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: A "Useless" Asset Class: Is Kashkari's Skepticism Toward Cryptocurrency Justified?
detail.abstract: Minneapolis Federal Reserve President Neel Kashkari has been one of the most persistent institutional critics of cryptocurrency, culminating in his February 2026 declaration that digital assets are “utterly useless.” This essay examines the intellectual foundations of Kashkari’s critique, which centers on cryptocurrency’s failure to satisfy the classical functions of money and its inability to displace existing payment infrastructure such as Venmo or Zelle. It then evaluates the principal counterarguments, including the deployment of stablecoins in cross-border business payments by firms such as Payoneer, remittance market adoption via MoneyGram’s USDC-based application in Colombia, divergent views among Federal Reserve officials, and the regulatory clarity provided by the GENIUS Act of 2025. The essay concludes that while Kashkari’s challenge remains substantive, emerging operational evidence suggests his categorical dismissal may require refinement as the technology matures.

title: The Cyclicality of Direct Lending
affiliations: , ,  and Frankfurt School of Finance & Management

detail.title: The Cyclicality of Direct Lending
detail.abstract: In direct lending, nonbank financial institutions originate bilaterally negotiated loans to risky firms. We document that issuance in this segment of the private credit market is countercyclical relative to issuance in other high-yield corporate credit markets, such as syndicated loans. This countercyclicality is the result of firms substituting across credit markets. Rather than forgo debt financing, firms switch to direct lending when credit conditions in other credit markets tighten. This substitution behavior is especially pronounced among sponsor-backed firms. Contrary to the concern that private credit could amplify credit supply shocks, our results indicate that private credit may dampen the corporate credit cycle. Thus, our findings have important implications for assessing the financial stability ramifications of the rapid growth in private credit.

title: Realized Regularized Regressions
affiliations: University of Manchester - Manchester Business School and University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance

detail.title: Realized Regularized Regressions
detail.abstract: Financial datasets are expanding rapidly, with an increasing number of variables observed at high frequencies. This raises challenges for estimation and variable selection in high-frequency regressions within a high-dimensional environment. We develop a continuous-time penalized regression framework for the estimation of time-varying coefficients when both the response and covariates are Itô semimartingales with jumps. The coefficient paths are approximated by spline basis expansions and estimated via least squares from truncated high-frequency increments. In a finite-dimensional setting, we establish consistency and derive a feasible asymptotic distribution for the integrated coefficient estimator under infill asymptotics. We then extend the framework to high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate covariates diverges, and show that a group-wise penalized estimator with a truncated L1-penalty attains the oracle property, which delivers both consistent model selection and coefficient estimation. An empirical application to a large panel of more than two hundred high-frequency factors investigates sparse factor structure across a large cross-section of stocks and industry portfolios.

title: Can Reputation Substitute for Enforcement? International Conservation Labels and Deforestation
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), Department of Economics

detail.title: Can Reputation Substitute for Enforcement? International Conservation Labels and Deforestation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no conflict of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N.A.
declarations.funderStatement: I receive no funding.

detail.abstract: Can international monitoring without enforcement power protect the environment? I study this question using UNESCO World Heritage inscription, which layers international visibility, monitoring, and reputational stakes onto protected areas without changing domestic legal protection. Exploiting staggered inscription timing across 276 natural and mixed sites and satellite-based deforestation data from 2001-2024, I estimate the causal effect of this international label on forest loss. Inscription reduces annual deforestation by 0.057 to 0.099 percentage points, with the largest effects in tropical regions where pressure is greatest. For a median tropical site, this implies roughly 620 hectares of avoided forest loss per year and about 160,000 tonnes of avoided CO2 emissions. While World Heritage sites face more documented attempts to weaken protection, they show lower enacted reversal rates than comparable domestic protected areas, consistent with reputational pressure raising the political cost of policy reversal. The protective effect peaks three to five years after inscription and spills over up to 10 km beyond site boundaries. These results show that international monitoring regimes can strengthen domestic conservation commitments even without formal enforcement authority.

title: Digital Cash, Transaction Scale, and the Institutional Economics of Payment Security
affiliations: University of Exeter

detail.title: Digital Cash, Transaction Scale, and the Institutional Economics of Payment Security
detail.abstract: Recent theoretical work analyses blockchain security at the consensus layer under assumptions of anonymous participants, frictionless entry, zero sunk costs, and no institutional enforcement. Those assumptions describe a limiting case. Payment-system security decomposes into three layers: transaction-level script conditions, consensus-level deterrence, and institutional enforcement. The layer containing the binding operational constraint varies by transaction class. For cost-disproportion transactions ($1$500), attack cost exceeds transaction value by a factor of 10 7 or more; the consensus-cost result does not bind. For script-conditioned transfers ($1K$1M), the result does not apply to the conditional release, whose operative constraint is script design; it applies to the funding transaction. For institutionally-enforced settlement ($1M and above), the result is supplemented by Beckerian deterrence where operators are identiable and legally reachable. For tokenised securities, it does not apply: security derives from the regulatory framework.

title: The New Hampshire Bitcoin-Backed Municipal Bond: Innovation, Structure, and a Quantitative Case for Caution
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The New Hampshire Bitcoin-Backed Municipal Bond: Innovation, Structure, and a Quantitative Case for Caution
detail.abstract: The proposed $100 million Bitcoin-backed municipal bond issued through the New Hampshire Business Finance Authority represents a novel intersection of public finance and digital asset markets. Structured as a conduit financing, the bond is supported solely by Bitcoin collateral provided by a private borrower, with no recourse to state funds or taxpayers. Proponents argue that the transaction expands capital access and positions New Hampshire as a leader in financial innovation. However, the structure raises significant concerns related to collateral volatility, liquidation triggers, and operational execution. This study evaluates the bond's legal design, economic rationale, and risk profile, supported by a quantitative analysis of Bitcoin price behavior from January 2024 through March 2026. Historical backtesting indicates that liquidation thresholds would have been triggered in a majority of potential issuance scenarios, while Monte Carlo simulation suggests an extremely high probability of forced liquidation within a two-year horizon under observed volatility conditions. The findings indicate that the instrument exhibits characteristics more consistent with speculative structured credit than traditional municipal finance. The paper concludes that the bond is best understood as a bespoke financing mechanism rather than a scalable innovation, with important implications for policymakers, investors, and regulators.

title: The CLARITY Act and Polymarket: A Controlled Econometric Analysis of Bitcoin Price Sensitivity
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The CLARITY Act and Polymarket: A Controlled Econometric Analysis of Bitcoin Price Sensitivity
detail.abstract: This paper empirically examines the relationship between Polymarket prediction market odds for the passage of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act (CLARITY Act) and the price of Bitcoin, while controlling for broader equity market movements. Using daily data from January 1 to April 4, 2026 (94 observations), the analysis first confirms that Bitcoin log-returns and changes in Polymarket odds are stationary (Augmented Dickey-Fuller p < .01). A multiple linear regression reveals that the Nasdaq Composite Index strongly drives Bitcoin returns (b = 1.71, p < .001). The CLARITY Act odds change shows a positive but weakly significant effect (b = 0.0022, p = .132). Granger causality tests find no short-term predictability at lags 1 through 5. These results suggest that while legislative sentiment aligns with Bitcoin valuation over longer horizons, the dominant driver of Bitcoin returns is equity market risk appetite, and Polymarket does not provide a reliable shortterm trading signal.

title: Judicial Delocalization and Corporate Tax Avoidance: Evidence from China's Circuit Tribunal Reform
affiliations: , Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management and Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management

detail.title: Judicial Delocalization and Corporate Tax Avoidance: Evidence from China's Circuit Tribunal Reform
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of judicial delocalization on corporate tax avoidance by exploiting the staggered establishment of cross-provincial Circuit Tribunals in China as a quasi-natural experiment. We find that judicial delocalization significantly reduces corporate tax avoidance, with the effect concentrated among firms lacking political connections. The channel analyses indicates that the reform imposes a binding enforcement discipline on financially constrained firms by strengthening judicial credibility and substitute weak local governance arrangements. Additionally, we also find that the deterrent effect of the reform is more pronounced for firms that were more embedded in local protectionist environments prior to the reform, including older firms and firms with longer operating cycles. Our study highlights the importance of the spatial organization of judicial authority in shaping enforcement credibility and provides new evidence that judicial delocalization can serve as an effective institutional mechanism for curbing corporate tax avoidance in emerging economies.

title: Cyber Hygiene as a Cornerstone of Cybersecurity Resilience in Cameroon and Sub-Saharan Africa: A Conceptual Review and Proposed National Framework
affiliations: Highstone International University, Highstone International University, Charisma University and University of Yaounde 1

detail.title: Cyber Hygiene as a Cornerstone of Cybersecurity Resilience in Cameroon and Sub-Saharan Africa: A Conceptual Review and Proposed National Framework
detail.abstract: Amid Cameroon's accelerating digital economy-marked by surging mobile money transactions, e-governance adoption, and expanding internet penetration-cyber threats have escalated dramatically across both public and private sectors. Data from the National Agency for Information and Communication Technologies (ANTIC) for 2025 reveals 32,500 judicial requisitions (a 30% increase from 2024, averaging nearly 200 daily), 8,502 detected vulnerabilities since January 2024, 206 digital evidence authentication reports, and widespread fake account proliferation (8,499 detected, with 6,416 removed). Financial losses from cybercrime in the banking sector alone exceeded CFA 1.027 billion in documented cases, with 471 scamming and phishing incidents and 59 fraudulent investment platforms identified. This paper conceptualizes *cyber hygiene*-routine, proactive practices including strong authentication, regular patching, secure backups, and sustained awareness-as an essential, low-cost foundation for national cybersecurity resilience. Synthesizing African maturity assessments (e.g., GCSCC CMM reviews showing "start-up" or "formative" awareness levels in many nations, including Cameroon's 2019 World Bank-facilitated assessment) and Cameroonian empirical evidence, we highlight persistent gaps in executive buy-in, multi-stakeholder coordination, and digital literacy across population segments. We propose the **Cameroon Cyber Hygiene Framework (CCHF)**, a staged, multi-stakeholder model integrating NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions, CMM maturity dimensions, and local socio-technical realities. Recommendations focus on ANTIC-led national coordination, formal education integration at all levels, public-private partnerships for scalable delivery, and metrics-driven implementation to shift the national posture from reactive forensics toward proactive prevention. The framework positions cyber hygiene not as a technical luxury but as a developmental imperative for Cameroon and analogous Sub-Saharan African contexts.

title: The Diagonalization of Agency: A Thermodynamic Ontology of the Firm - Paper n.1
affiliations: University of São Paulo (USP)

detail.title: The Diagonalization of Agency: A Thermodynamic Ontology of the Firm - Paper n.1
detail.abstract: This essay proposes a provocative rupture in the understanding of the modern corporation, crossing the boundaries between institutional economics, evolutionary biology, and physics. Unlike the pure market, which dynamically processes information as a continuous and borderless flow, the modern firm has devolved into isolated epistemic fiefdoms. Consequently, it is argued that the true drain of value in contemporary enterprises does not stem from moral conflicts between principals and agents-as classical Agency Theory suggests-but from "epistemic latency": the severe informational friction and systemic paralysis generated by these hyper-specialized silos. Moving away from poetic analogies and employing direct isomorphisms with Shannon's information theory and Prigogine's dissipative structures, the text demonstrates that the firm operates strictly as a thermodynamic engine tasked with processing market entropy. As a structural antidote to this inefficiency, the Theory of the Diagonalization of Agency is formulated. At the center of this model emerges the Diagonal CEO: a Relevance Arbitrator who, armed with a multidisciplinary cognitive scaffold and the Socratic method, acts as an "impedance matching" interface between silos, converting informational noise into Net Temporal Value (NTV). The work culminates in an ineluctable thesis on the destiny of governance: the necessary metabolic transition of decision-making from carbon-structurally limited by biological heuristics and emotions-to the thermodynamic and allocative efficiency of silicon, consolidating Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) not merely as a tool, but as the ultimate frontier of corporate evolution.

title: The Body as Sovereign Asset: Solomon, Epstein, and the Political Economy of Sexualized Power

detail.title: The Body as Sovereign Asset: Solomon, Epstein, and the Political Economy of Sexualized Power
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a structural theory of risk architecture in opaque convertibility systems. It argues that under specific administrative conditions, localized resources-such as embodied intimacy, kinship, access, or relational proximity-can be organized into infrastructures capable of translating influence across domains. These infrastructures generate yield by converting one form of capital into another: intimacy into alliance, alliance into protection, proximity into financial access, or shared exposure into compliance. 
     The analysis does not equate historical regimes nor reduce complex systems to individual pathology. Instead, it isolates a recurring architectural configuration: inventory accumulation, controlled circulation, strategic allocation, and opacity mediation. When these subsystems converge, convertibility produces integrative effects that may resemble sovereign capacity. 
     The paper develops a structural model in which relational density increases yield polynomially but increases exposure probability nonlinearly, while opacity mechanisms exhibit diminishing marginal absorption. Structural instability emerges when marginal risk growth exceeds marginal yield growth. The critical threshold is determined by relational density, opacity capacity, and institutional exposure intensity. 
     Two asymmetrical illustrations-a dynastic diplomatic monarchy preserved in sacral historiography and a contemporary relational-financial network documented through legal recordsdemonstrate how identical subsystem logics operate under divergent archival and oversight ecologies. The comparison is architectural rather than moral or empirical parity-based. 
     The central claim is that opaque convertibility infrastructures are inherently bounded by nonlinear exposure dynamics. Their expansion is economically tempting but structurally selflimiting. Collapse, when it occurs, reflects saturation of opacity capacity rather than sudden moral deviation. Recognizing this architecture reframes episodes of scandal or fragmentation as threshold events within systems whose risk accelerates faster than their integrative yield. The model is conceptual rather than econometric: it generates qualitative predictions about system behavior under specified conditions and is falsifiable by cases in which the four subsystems converge without producing cross-domain convertibility, or in which scaling does not produce the predicted nonlinear exposure dynamics.

title: Perverse Effects of Imperfectly Enforced Price Controls
affiliations: and Corvinus University of Budapest

detail.title: Perverse Effects of Imperfectly Enforced Price Controls
detail.abstract: We study the effects of a rent control policy when enforcement relies on tenant complaints rather than government monitoring. We show theoretically that when tenants differ in their ability to enforce the rent cap, adverse selection arises: landlords set rents anticipating how enforcement risk depends on the composition of tenants. Higher listed rents deter tenants who are unlikely to enforce the cap, increasing enforcement risk and inducing further rent increases. The resulting equilibrium rents are higher than in the no regulation benchmark and depend negatively on the rent cap level. Using rental listings data from Vienna between 2012 and 2022, we test the model's predictions by exploiting policy changes and institutional variation in rent caps. We find that tighter rent control leads to 76 EUR higher posted rents on average, consistent with our theoretical predictions.

title: Anatomy of Subjective Macroeconomic Expectations *
affiliations: Northwestern University and Northwestern University - Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences

detail.title: Anatomy of Subjective Macroeconomic Expectations *
detail.abstract: We develop a structural approach to identify latent belief shocks underlying the cross-sectional subjective macroeconomic expectations system, combining sign restrictions with narrative identification. Departing from existing literature that studies expectations one outcome at a time, we provide a unified anatomy of expectation comovement while remaining agnostic about underlying microfoundations. Contrary to the conventional supply-side view, we show that a pessimism shock-a broad adverse shift in beliefs across macroeconomic outcomes-accounts for the dominant share of covariance in households expectations, extending well beyond output and inflation. We further map these belief shocks to observable heterogeneity, showing that pessimism is concentrated among individuals with low income, unemployment, deteriorating financial conditions, and poor health, who anticipate lower future earnings, higher job-loss and default risk, and plan to dissave.

title: Geopolitical Risks and Financial Stability: How to Assess the Risks
affiliations: University of Zurich - Rechtswissenschaftliches Institut (School of Law)

detail.title: Geopolitical Risks and Financial Stability: How to Assess the Risks
detail.abstract: This paper analyses some of the main linkages between geopolitical risks and financial market stability. It also discusses how financial regulators perceive geopolitical risks and how they should address the related systemic risks. The paper discusses how geopolitical risks are impacting the cross-border operations of large banks and the transmission channels for such risks.  The paper considers the Sberbank AG case and how the application of financial sanctions against its Russian parent bank led to a loss of liquidity for the Russian bank’s European subsidiaries and the decision by EU authorities to put the European subsidiaries into resolution. The article concludes that although geo-political risks should be monitored and factored into regulatory and supervisory strategies, state fiscal interventions have mitigated the negative impact on financial markets. However, the growing use of fiscal and other governmental measures may not be sustainable over the longer term.

title: Competing Powers *
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics and Columbia University in the City of New York

detail.title: Competing Powers *
detail.abstract: Motivated by the growing interest in geoeconomics, we develop a formal framework in which multiple superpowers-such as the United States and China-compete to shape the behavior of less powerful countries or firms. We model superpowers as competing principals who influence an agent's policy choice by threatening costly punishments. We characterize the set of equilibrium policy choices as a system of incentive-compatibility constraints on each actor. Equilibrium policy choices tend to favor more powerful principals, and larger policy concessions can be extracted when principals are more aligned. When all parties additionally have access to frictionless transfers, Coasian surplus-maximizing equilibria always exist regardless of the distribution of punishment power, with power impacting only the division of surplus. However, this result no longer holds if frictions are introduced.

title: Environmental Information as a Public Utility

detail.title: Environmental Information as a Public Utility
detail.abstract:
This preprint argues that current ESG and CSRD sustainability governance is structurally inefficient because it relies on decentralized, document-heavy compliance. Thousands of firms independently reproduce similar data collection, auditing, and reporting processes, which creates duplicated costs, fragmented datasets, and high administrative overhead. As a result, a growing share of resources is absorbed by compliance itself rather than by real environmental improvements.

The paper reframes sustainability reporting as a system-level resource allocation problem. Compliance is treated as a measurable system cost that competes with actual decarbonization and transition investments. When reporting, assurance, and validation are duplicated across firms, regulatory “entropy” increases and net environmental outcomes deteriorate, even if formal rules become stricter.

To address this, the paper proposes a structural shift toward an Environmental Information Utility model, also described as “Regulatory-as-a-Service.” In this model, the regulator (or a delegated public institution) operates a shared information infrastructure that produces standardized, validated, machine-readable environmental indices. Firms provide only minimal incremental inputs, while reusable outputs are distributed through stable APIs.

Two core indices are introduced. The Environmental Load Index represents a fact-based environmental footprint aligned with lifecycle assessment principles. The Improvement Potential Index represents the feasible reduction potential under known technologies and constraints. These indices are designed to be directly consumable by financial systems, procurement platforms, and consumer tools.

By centralizing the label and index layer, the system reduces transaction costs, improves comparability, limits rating divergence and greenwashing, and enables continuous, AI-driven decision-making. Quantitative illustrations show that as duplicated compliance overhead declines, net environmental gain increases mechanically, even under uncertainty.

The paper also outlines a practical implementation architecture, governance safeguards, and a concrete pilot roadmap. It argues that treating environmental information as a digital public utility aligns sustainability regulation with how modern markets, algorithms, and institutions actually operate, shifting the focus from paperwork compliance to measurable environmental impact.

title: The Zero-Sum Game of Mutual Fund Marketing

detail.title: The Zero-Sum Game of Mutual Fund Marketing
detail.abstract: We analyze the role of social media livestreams by mutual fund families as a marketing tool. We find that these livestreams do not attract new money or increase fee revenue at the family level because they primarily reallocate flows within the family: featured funds experience significant inflows, offset by significant outflows from non-featured funds. Featured funds significantly outperform non-featured funds in the months leading up to a livestream, and this outperformance dissipates around the livestream and reverses into slight underperformance thereafter. Our results are consistent with families using livestreams to retain investors in underperforming funds by steering them toward better-performing alternatives within the family, reducing incentives to search outside the family. Using a large language model to analyze 795 transcripts of livestreams that do attract substantial family-level new money, we find that they emphasize "hard information" (past performance and third-party validation) over emotional appeals or engagement tactics.

detail.title: Thinking versus Doing: Cognitive Capacity, Decision Making and Medical Diagnosis

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study how situational fluctuations in cognitive capacity shape behavior in high-stakes, real-time decision-making. Drawing on recent advances in behavioral economics that revolve around inattention, cognition and complexity, we show that cognitive load influences how physicians in emergency departments allocate mental effort and attention when making diagnostic and treatment decisions. We use quasi-random variation in patient-physician pairings, along with granular electronic medical record and audit-log data from many clinical interactions, to show that, under higher cognitive load, physicians substitute mental deliberation with more numerous but less precise diagnostic actions. Specifically, we document that higher load (i) increases the total number of orders of diagnostic tests (ii) reduces the use of targeted, but more uncommon tests (iii) increases the use of common tests and (iv) increases uncertainty in diagnostic beliefs. Cognitive load impacts downstream inpatient admission from the emergency department: a physician in the highest cognitive load decile increases admissions by 28% relative to the same physician in the lowest cognitive load decile, for the exact same kind of patient. These results offer novel field-based evidence on the dynamics of attention and belief formation, and shed light on how cognitive constraints shape diagnostic behavior in complex, real-world environments.
