detail.abstract:
On March 15, 2021, a senior hedge fund analyst was tasked with formulating an investment thesis for AMC Entertainment (AMC). The stock had been highly volatile as the US economy emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic and markets grappled with the pandemic's impact on future consumer behavior. AMC's stock price, which had slumped from $7 to $2 at the onset of the pandemic and had been hovering around $4 for months, had skyrocketed to nearly $20 in a few trading sessions in January 2021.There were compelling arguments both for betting on AMC appreciating even further and for betting on its demise. On one hand, investor optimism about the cinema chain was understandable: vaccines were rolling out, and markets were confident in the US economy's swift return to normalcy. On the other hand, even in the most optimistic scenarios, the $14.04 price at which AMC traded on March 15, 2021, seemed far removed from the company's fundamentals. To complicate matters, the presence of retail investors betting on “meme” stocks added significant volatility to select stocks, including AMC.This public-sourced case uses fundamental analysis as a starting point for students to explore the mechanics, costs, and risks of short investing strategies. It has been successfully taught at the University of Virginia Darden School of Business in the “Enterprise Valuation” module of “Financial Management and Policies,” a first-year core course in the MBA program. The case has also been used in the first- and second-year elective, “Valuation in Financial Markets.” Since the case covers both valuation methodologies and option pricing, it has also served as a capstone for the first-year core finance course.

Excerpt

AMC: A Short Story

On March 15, 2021, Ruth Karasu, a senior analyst for EDN Management's Gallatin Fund (Gallatin), a midsize hedge fund, was in her makeshift work-from-home office, looking incredulously at the share price of AMC Entertainment Holdings, Inc. (AMC). She had been tasked with assessing how the fund could profit from the recent wild moves in the stock price of the country's largest cinema company. The lockdown orders of March 2020 had forced AMC to shut down its theaters, causing its stock price to drop from $7 to an all-time low of $2 per share. Less than a year later, however, AMC's price had soared to new heights: it registered the single largest one-day gain in its almost-10-year history of being a public company on January 27, 2021, when the price jumped 301%, from $4.96 to $19.90, and it was still trading at twice its pre-COVID level on March 15, at $14.04 (Exhibit 1).

As AMC was a company whose business relied on in-person experiences, its valuation would soar in the middle of a global pandemic only if its future fundamental revenue drivers shifted significantly. Karasu thought the stock-price numbers might reflect a market increasingly optimistic about future cinema attendance and a swifter-than-expected return to normalcy. The latest statistics on vaccine rollouts Karasu had gathered pointed in that direction, showing an acceleration in pace, with 125 million doses administered in the three months since the beginning of the year. The newly immunized public was ready to spend: just a few days before, Barclays Bank Plc (Barclays) CEO Jes Staley had compared the pent-up demand in the global economy to that following the end of the 1918 flu. Perhaps the “roaring '20s” were likelier than Karasu had originally thought.

The recent spikes in AMC's stock price might also be driven by a less rational explanation. Just a few months earlier, in January 2021, the market had marveled at the stock price of Gamestop Corp. (Gamestop; stock trading symbols: GME), which had skyrocketed “to the moon,” as the online traders who fueled the price hike often put it. These day traders bought the stock in a frenzy, having coordinated in an obscure online community board to increase the video game retailer's price and drive hedge funds out of business. The fact that the stock prices of AMC's competitors had not increased nearly as much as AMC's had (Exhibit 1) suggested that this “retail traders” explanation could be a possibility.

title: Strengthening Anti-Money Laundering Safeguards in U.S. Immigration Programs: Regulatory Gaps and Policy Solutions for Protecting Financial Integrity

detail.title: Strengthening Anti-Money Laundering Safeguards in U.S. Immigration Programs: Regulatory Gaps and Policy Solutions for Protecting Financial Integrity
detail.abstract:
The globalization of migration has increasingly intersected with international financial flows. Immigration systems, particularly those involving investment migration, employment sponsorship, and cross-border financial transfers serve as legitimate channels for economic mobility, labor market development, and international cooperation. At the same time, these
systems may inadvertently create opportunities for illicit financial activity. Money laundering remains one of the most persistent threats to financial integrity worldwide, as criminal actors attempt to disguise the origin of unlawful proceeds by integrating them into legitimate economic systems. The United States maintains one of the most sophisticated anti–money laundering (AML) frameworks globally, primarily through statutory mechanisms such as the Bank Secrecy Act and related financial reporting requirements administered by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. Despite these regulatory mechanisms, immigration programs are not always fully integrated into the broader financial compliance framework. Certain immigration pathways involve significant financial transfers and business investments, which may create potential vulnerabilities if oversight mechanisms are insufficient. This article examines the intersection between U.S. immigration programs and anti–money laundering enforcement. It identifies structural regulatory gaps, including challenges in verifying foreign sources of wealth, limited financial monitoring obligations for certain professional intermediaries, and institutional coordination barriers among government agencies. The article further proposes policy reforms designed to strengthen financial transparency while preserving the economic and humanitarian benefits of immigration. Enhanced interagency collaboration, improved due diligence mechanisms, and the integration of financial intelligence tools into immigration oversight could significantly strengthen the integrity of the U.S. immigration system.

detail.abstract: Why do some political regimes endure while others collapse? I argue regimes belong to institutional lineages, and path-dependent design features shape survival. Using regime-type episodes (1789-2024) and Bayesian phylogenetic survival models, I show that income and democracy effects largely disappear once institutional ancestry is modeled. detail.title: Contractual Private Disclosures in Supply Chains and Managerial Learning from Financial Markets
detail.abstract: I examine whether contracts that require customers to privately share with suppliers forecasts of their future demand for the supplier's products (“demand forecast contracts,” or “DF contracts”) affect the supplier’s reliance on an alternative information source — stock prices — when making investment decisions. If suppliers find these forecasts a more direct signal of future demand than stock prices, they may reduce their reliance on stock prices to guide investments. Using hand-collected data, I find that suppliers’ investments become significantly less sensitive to stock prices after entering a DF contract for the first time. This effect is stronger when forecasts are more credible, demand more uncertain, and investments more irreversible. Supplier performance, measured by return on assets and cash flow from operations, improves post-DF. Overall, these findings suggest that when a relatively direct information source about future demand becomes available, managers reduce their reliance on stock prices in making real decisions.

detail.title: The Wagner Protocol: A Behavioral Model of Identity Reconstruction and Reinvention
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Wagner Protocol, a proposed behavioral model describing how individuals reconstruct identity following disruption or collapse of an existing life structure. While reinvention is commonly described through narrative and anecdotal accounts, it is rarely defined through structured behavioral stages and there is limited structured language for understanding its underlying behavioral patterns. Drawing on repeated real-world observations across multiple environments and life transitions, aligned with existing concepts in identity development and post traumatic growth (Tedeschi & Calhoun, 2004), the model identifies a consistent four-stage sequence: Ground Zero, Stormfront, Breakthrough, and Rise. The framework is not presented as a universal law, but as a structured model for understanding commonly observed patterns in identity reconstruction.

detail.title: From Ad Hoc to Optimised: Maturity, Adoption and the Governance of AI-Enabled Assurance
detail.abstract: The first two papers in this series established the theoretical and architectural case for continuous AI-enabled assurance: that static governance cannot reliably control dynamic systems, and that multi-agent orchestrated AI provides the computational architecture for assurance commensurate with the complexity of contemporary public programs. This concluding paper addresses the practical question that those arguments defer: how do organisations build this capability, starting from where they are? Two frameworks are advanced as generic contributions to the field. First, an AI Assurance Maturity Model — a five-dimension, five-level diagnostic framework providing a structured vocabulary for organisations to assess their current capability and plan their progression. Second, a phased adoption pathway that translates readiness into an ordered implementation sequence with defined entry conditions and phase completion signals. The paper also argues, drawing on implementation failure research and organisational change theory, that the preconditions for successful adoption are systematically underestimated across three dimensions — data quality, technical integration and organisational readiness — and that deployment sequencing must reflect these realities rather than assumed starting conditions. Finally, it argues that the governance of the AI system itself is not a separate topic to be addressed after adoption is complete but a precondition of assurance legitimacy that must be established before deployment begins. The frameworks are offered as field-level contributions available for adaptation and empirical testing independent of any specific commercial platform.

English Abstract: >What are the implications of the intersection between the politics of fear and pandemic politics? This article investigates this dynamic through existentialist, theoretical, and empirical lenses, employing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. While human mortality is a universal certainty, its timing and nature remain fundamentally unknown. This study questions whether the consciousness of death remains a private concern or if it possesses a distinct role within the public sphere. Specifically, we explore the consequences that arise when the awareness of mortality is politicized. We examine how pandemic politics have leveraged mass existential anxiety, identifying an unprecedented global surge in mortality discourse and analyzing the role of political actors in both fostering and exploiting this phenomenon. To conceptualize these dynamics, we propose an innovative model that categorizes governmental responses along a spectrum between the "Oak" (characterized by steadfast resistance) and the "Reed" (representing flexible resilience). We find that political trust, a higher median age, and social anxiety are primary predictors of the Reed approach; that the oak strategy – which typically favors more stringent measures – demonstrates greater efficacy in reducing overall mortality; and that policy severity in and of itself shows a negligible impact on COVID–19 morbidity and mortality rates. The model is grounded in the experiences of five nations: China and Israel (Oaks), Sweden and Germany (Reeds), and the United States (an Oak–Reed hybrid).

detail.abstract: Introduction: Trauma is a leading cause of global mortality and has been influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic. The interaction between trauma seasonality and pandemic effects remains understudied. From an AI modeling perspective, understanding seasonal shifts over the last four years is critical to training reliable models. Methods: We performed a retrospective study of 33,945 trauma admissions from 2014–2024 at a single Level I trauma center. Demographics, injury characteristics, and transfusion data were analyzed alongside weather and environmental variables including temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, dew point, visibility, barometric pressure, workday status, and solar length. Statistical analyses included Chi-square, Cragg-Uhler, McFadden, AIC, and BIC. Results: Solar length was the strongest predictor of admissions, with longer days associated with increased trauma volume. This effect intensified after 2020 and remained elevated post-pandemic. Ground-level falls and MVCs increased, while ISS decreased. XGBoost performed well on training data (R² = 0.66, MAE = 1.75). Discussion: Seasonality strengthened after 2020, and trauma admissions remain directly proportional to solar length. AI models using this metric accurately forecast admissions over 60-day intervals.

detail.title: Numeraire-Based Distributional Sensitivity Engine for European Options under Stochastic Interest Rates
detail.abstract:
Distributional Sensitivity Engine (DSE) organizes European option prices and sensitivities for equity diffusions with deterministic term structures by rewriting the in-the-money event through a Doleans-Dade exponential. The price is expressed in the two-weight form V_t=w_1*a_1+w_2*a_2 , where (a_1, a_2) are F_t -measurable primitives and (w_1, w_2) are conditional digital quantities under two measures linked by a Girsanov tilt. A limitation of DSE is the assumption that discounting is F_t -measurable. 
This paper presents an extension of that representation to European options under stochastic interest rates. A central step normalizes the discount factor by the bond price B(t,T)=E_t^Q [DF_(t,T)]. This normalization yields an F_t -measurable exercise boundary for a modified Doleans-Dade log variable E_(t,T). The spot leg remains under the Doleans tilt measure Q^+ , while the strike leg is written through a digital weight under the T-forward measure, or more generally under a suitable numeraire measure. The resulting representation retains the basic engine structure. In particular, it retains a two-weight price representation and a four-input contraction form for first derivatives. The probabilistic core is therefore reduced to conditional distribution blocks under Q^+ and Q^T. Dirac-delta representations are then used to construct Monte Carlo estimators for CDF, PDF, and derivative blocks, and a mollified delta yields estimators with the standard bias-variance scaling associated with kernel smoothing.

detail.abstract: We estimate the effect of LED street-lighting modernization on crime in São Paulo, Brazil. Using administrative records on lighting infrastructure and geocoded police reports, we construct a high-resolution spatial panel of grid cells and define treatment by the first observed LED installation within each cell. The main empirical design compares cells first treated in 2018Q3 to cells that remain untreated through 2020Q1, using the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) difference-indifferences framework. We find economically large declines in cellphone theft, especially at night, with the strongest evidence concentrated in outcomes for which event-study diagnostics do not reject parallel trends. Vehicle-related crime also tends to decline after treatment, although the corresponding pre-trend evidence is weaker. Daytime placebo results suggest that part of the estimated effect may reflect correlated neighborhood-level changes rather than lighting alone. Overall, the findings indicate that LED modernization is associated with meaningful reductions in some property-crime outcomes, while also highlighting the identification challenges involved in evaluating large-scale urban infrastructure interventions.

title: Recency Effect of Weather Shocks on Fertilizer Adoption: Evidence from Nigeria

detail.title: Recency Effect of Weather Shocks on Fertilizer Adoption: Evidence from Nigeria
detail.abstract: I examine whether recency bias-forming expectations from recent experiences-induced by recent rainfall shocks reduces fertilizer use among maize farmers in Nigeria. Economic theory predicts that a profit-maximizing farmer should not be influenced by recent weather shocks except through liquidity constraints. Using nationally representative panel data merged with historical rainfall data, I show that, conditional on past profit (proxied by livestock accumulation and prior season's maize price), recent rainfall shocks significantly influence current fertilizer use even though shocks are serially uncorrelated and transitory. Importantly, I find that this effect is negatively asymmetric: prior negative shocks depress fertilizer use more than prior positive shocks raise it, thereby lowering average fertilizer use. Back-of-the-envelope calculations imply that weather-induced recency bias is associated with about 5% reduction in the already low fertilizer use (56.2 kg/acre) in Nigeria. Improving access to accurate and timely weather forecasts could help households make more efficient input use decisions.

detail.abstract: Local projections (LPs) are often viewed as a flexible alternative to vector autoregressions (VARs), while VARs are often seen as better suited to imposing additional structure. This paper shows that the two are linked by an exact finite-sample identity. Its main result shows that, for any dataset, the h-step forecast from an LP of order p is exactly what one obtains by iterating forward through h one-step VAR forecasts, beginning with a VAR of order p and increasing the lag order by one at each iteration. Conversely, a VAR can be recovered from a corresponding sequence of LPs of decreasing order. The result strengthens the earlier population equivalence literature by moving to an exact finite-sample identity and explains the familiar finite-sample patterns in LP-VAR comparisons. It also extends to settings often seen as specific to either LPs or VARs, including single-equation LPs, panels, different lag lengths across variables, deterministic trends, vector error-correction representations, and common nonlinear or state-dependent specifications. Thus, in these settings, LPs are not inherently more flexible, nor are VARs inherently better suited to imposing structure.

detail.abstract: We study a finite-horizon dynamic wholesale-price contract between a manufacturer and a retailer, both of whom observe only sales, rather than the true demand. When the retailer stocks out, unmet demand is unobserved, so both parties update a common posterior over the demand distribution from sales data. Each period, the manufacturer sets the wholesale price, the retailer chooses an order quantity, and the public belief state is updated. We characterize Markov perfect equilibria as functions of this public belief. Our main results are as follows: for Weibull demand, we extend the well-known scaling approach to this strategic learning setting, prove the existence of an equilibrium, and reduce computation to a standardized one-parameter recursion; for exponential demand, we show that the equilibrium is unique and computable via a simple backward recursion.

detail.abstract: The practitioner toolkit for strategic decision-making—portfolio matrices, industry structure models, decision governance protocols, phased development gates—has expanded substantially over five decades, yet the reviewed academic literature has not yet produced a unified taxonomy for classifying these tools by structural properties and reassessing their fitness for purpose in an AI-transformed environment. Usage studies document adoption frequency without explaining architectural differences; the emerging AI-strategy literature examines cognitive processes without systematically assessing the toolkit itself. This paper addresses both gaps. Drawing on a corpus of 28 practitioner-originated frameworks selected by explicit inclusion criteria from MBA curricula, consulting firm methodologies, and strategy textbooks, it proposes a four-dimensional taxonomy classifying each tool by primary function (nine categories), decision layer (Strategy Formulation, Strategic Choice, Execution Governance, Operating Cadence), time horizon (ultra-short to long), and AI affordance profile. A standardized three-criterion rubric—input automation, judgment displacement, and assumption stability—is applied to assign each framework an AI-era rating of Enhanced, Challenged, or Disrupted. Three findings emerge. First, the practitioner toolkit contains a persistent but unacknowledged boundary between strategy formulation tools and decision-process tools that differ on every structural dimension examined. Second, the current toolkit is concentrated at long time horizons, precisely the temporal range where AI augmentation is least effective, revealing a structural gap in the framework inventory. Third, the dominant mode of AI's impact is not replacement but tension: 57% of frameworks are Challenged—requiring adaptation rather than abandonment—while only 4% are Disrupted. The taxonomy offers a structured logic for matching tools to decision contexts and locating where AI-driven redesign should concentrate.

title: The Option Paradox in Executive Decision-Making: Choice Overload, Decision Fatigue, and the Case for Strategic No-Go

detail.title: The Option Paradox in Executive Decision-Making: Choice Overload, Decision Fatigue, and the Case for Strategic No-Go

detail.abstract:
Strategic management theory conventionally treats option creation as welfare-improving: more alternatives imply richer opportunity sets and better outcomes. This paper challenges that assumption. Drawing on three convergent but largely isolated research streams—choice overload, decision fatigue, and strategic discontinuation—it identifies an inflection point beyond which additional options degrade rather than improve executive decision quality.

The paper advances three propositions. First, C-suite decision environments structurally tend to exceed the cognitive thresholds at which choice overload impairs judgment—not occasionally, but as a persistent feature of the role. Second, the sequential, multi-item nature of executive decision sessions amplifies overload through decision fatigue, producing compounding degradation across a session’s agenda. Third, structured strategic No-Go—the deliberate, criteria-based elimination of options—can create economic value under identifiable conditions by conserving cognitive resources for decisions where they matter most.

From these propositions, the paper derives four design principles for organizational decision load management and identifies boundary conditions under which No-Go destroys rather than creates value.

In this paper, “strategic No-Go” refers to the executive application of structured strategic discontinuation—the deliberate rejection of options based on predefined criteria rather than real-time judgment.

detail.abstract: Strategic due diligence produces voluminous analysis, yet, to the author's knowledge, a widely adopted standardized mechanism for converting that analysis into a locked verdict is not evident—Go, Conditional Go, Delay, or No—at the C-level. Fortune 500 firms lose an estimated $250 million annually to inefficient decision processes (McKinsey, 2019). This paper argues that the gap between analysis and action constitutes a structural failure, not a managerial one, and introduces Decision Lock, a verdict-based decision quality framework designed to close it. Within the reviewed academic and practitioner literature, the present review did not identify an established framework—academic or practitioner-originated—that converts post-due-diligence analysis into a locked categorical verdict for C-level strategic decisions. Decision Lock is proposed as a candidate framework for this gap. Limitations include zero Full Go verdicts, limited No-verdict coverage (one case), no post-decision outcome tracking, and pending transition to live internal-data cases.

detail.abstract: The global investment in workplace behavioral change has tripled over fifteen years without producing a corresponding improvement in outcomes. Behavior change retention in corporate learning and development (L&D) falls below 30% at 90 days-a figure that has remained structurally stable despite sustained increases in per-employee training expenditure. This paper argues that this failure is not a delivery failure. It is a category error. The dominant intervention category-personality assessment and knowledge transfer-is structurally incapable of reaching the layer where sustained behavioral change occurs. Drawing on convergent findings across cognitive psychology, developmental psychology, analytical psychology, and psychodrama theory, this paper defines a new category: the Behavioral Operating System (BOS). A BOS is distinguished from existing frameworks by its intervention target (the developmental and archetypal layer, not the self-reported surface), its diagnostic logic (pattern origin, not trait description), and its delivery requirement (cultural-psychological specificity, not universalized assessment). This paper establishes the definitional conditions for category membership, distinguishes BOS from adjacent categories, and identifies implications for institutional adoption and future empirical validation.

title: Are We Currently Experiencing the Fifth Industrial Revolution? The Case for Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Are We Currently Experiencing the Fifth Industrial Revolution? The Case for Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: Every Industrial Revolution in recorded history has been characterised by a singular enabling technology that restructured labour markets, reorganised production systems, and permanently altered the social and institutional architecture of society. This article advances the thesis that Artificial Intelligence (AI), encompassing large language models, generative AI systems, and autonomous agents that emerged in mature form between approximately 2017 and 2025, constitutes the defining technological catalyst of a Fifth Industrial Revolution. Drawing on historical analyses of prior industrial transitions, primary and peer-reviewed empirical literature, and current enterprise adoption data, the argument proceeds in four stages: (1) a definitional framework for what constitutes an industrial revolution is established from the historical record; (2) the four prior revolutions are mapped against this framework; (3) AI is evaluated against each criterion; and (4) the critical distinction between Industry 4.0 and Industry 5.0, a frequently conflated debate in both academic and practitioner discourse is resolved. The analysis concludes that AI meets every historical threshold for revolutionary classification and that this transition is not approaching but already underway.

title: Learning the Distance in Exponential Ranking Models
affiliations: and Stanford

detail.title: Learning the Distance in Exponential Ranking Models
detail.abstract: Rankings arise across a wide range of economic and computational settings, including preference aggregation, recommendation systems, and expert evaluation. In many of these environments, ranking data are generated under domain-specific constraints, and different settings exhibit fundamentally different patterns of noise. We propose a class of exponential family models on permutations in which this noise structure is learned directly from data. Specifically, we introduce the learned-distance exponential ranking (LDER), a generalization of the classical Mallows model in which the distance itself is parameterized and learned. Under this model, a ranking π has likelihood proportional to expβ d α (π, σ) , where σ is a central ranking, β > 0 controls dispersion, and the distance parameter α governs the relative prevalence of long-range versus local deviations. To our knowledge, this is the first extension of the Mallows framework that learns the distance metric jointly with the central ranking and dispersion. We develop an efficient maximum likelihood procedure that jointly estimates (σ, α, β), prove strong consistency of the central ranking estimator, and establish √ m-consistency and asymptotic normality for (α, β), including robustness to approximate score computation. To enable distributional queries and simulation, we give a provably efficient approximation scheme for α ≥ 1 that, in time polynomial in n and 1/ε, produces a (1 ± ε) approximation to the partition function and an ε-total-variation sampler. Our learning and sampling algorithms generalize prior results even in the classical cases of fixed distance metric, α = 1 (Spearman footrule) and α = 2 (Spearman's ρ), where previous theoretical guarantees were given only in the vanishing-dispersion regime β → 0. Finally, we evaluate our approach on sports rankings, news and movie preference data.

At present, E-CNY has been piloted in many cities and has driven innovation in currency form; therefore, it is of great significance to explore the main factors driving users from third-party payment to switch to E-CNY, as well as the mechanisms driving E-CNY adoption. Based on the push-pull-mooring model, the study systematically analyses the factors influencing users’ switching from third-party payment tools to E-CNY. It empirically analyses 386 valid questionnaire responses using a partial least squares structural equation model. The study finds that push factors (privacy concerns, dissatisfaction with the quality of third-party payment tools) and pull factors (perceived ease of use, trust, and comparative advantage) significantly affect users’ intention to switch; mooring factors (switching costs, subjective norms, and habit) significantly affect users’ intention to switch; and mooring factors negatively regulate the relationship between push, pull factors, and intention to switch. detail.abstract: AI agent systems capable of autonomous action across enterprise environments are rapidly transitioning from research prototypes to production deployments. These systems inherit ambient credentials, operate nondeterministically, and lack standard mechanisms for binding actions to human identity-creating a security posture fundamentally incompatible with enterprise governance requirements. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for identity-aware agent governance addressing five critical gaps in current architectures: (1) ambient authority elimination through identity-inherited permissions, (2) infrastructure-level policy enforcement independent of model compliance, (3) sequence-aware authorization that detects composition attacks within authorized scope, (4) independent action verification addressing the oracle problem of agents selfreporting their own actions, and (5) hallucination-aware audit systems that account for LLM reasoning unreliability. We ground our analysis in documented vulnerabilities from production agent systems including the ClawHavoc supply chain attack (824+ malicious agent skills), Cisco's finding that 26% of analyzed agent skills contain security vulnerabilities, and architectural analysis of credential inheritance patterns in Claude Code Agent Teams, Cursor FastRender (2,000 concurrent agents), and OpenClaw (30,000+ internet-exposed instances). We evaluate the applicability of existing standards (OAuth 2.0, SPIFFE/SPIRE, Zero Trust Architecture, MCP) and identify specific extensions required for non-deterministic agent workflows. Our central contribution is a layered identity model with cryptographic delegation tokens that propagates human authorization through multi-agent chains, enabling per-call policy evaluation at the infrastructure layer. This work was developed concurrently with a public comment submission to the NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence initiative on Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization (2026).

detail.abstract: Expert networks are structured intermediaries that facilitate primary research consultations between institutional clients and independent industry professionals. Over the past three decades, expert networks have evolved from informal advisory matching services into structured, governance-embedded research infrastructure integrated within institutional investment workflows. Initially developed to facilitate access to industry practitioners for primary research purposes, expert networks now operate at global scale with formalized oversight systems, standardized engagement protocols, digital knowledge management platforms, and increasingly sophisticated technology integration. detail.abstract: Digital governance systems increasingly rely on infrastructures that execute and enforce decisions through pre-specified algorithmic mechanisms rather than contemporaneous institutional deliberation. Once such triggers are met, execution occurs at infrastructural tempo, often within seconds or less. Institutional review processes-deliberation, voting, sanction, or regulatory intervention-operate at materially slower timescales. The paper operationalizes this mechanism through a qualitative diagnostic framework that classifies enforcement and review tempos into empirically grounded bins and evaluates governance architectures across four dimensions: actor-forum coupling, temporal alignment, cross-layer visibility, and metarule integration. Structured application to oracle-mediated liquidation cascades, cross-chain infrastructure failures, and token-based governance systems demonstrate differentiated accountability profiles rather than uniform fragility. The findings suggest that accountability in algorithmic infrastructures is not eliminated by automation but reconfigured as an architectural property dependent upon tempo alignment and bridging capacity. Governance design implications are derived for prospective accountability integration, cross-layer forum specification, and tempo-aware regulatory oversight. By reframing digital governance as a problem of temporal and infrastructural alignment rather than decentralization rhetoric, the paper offers a diagnostic instrument for policy analysis in highspeed institutional environments.

title: How Much Customization Can a Production System Promise? The Case of Flow-Shops Under Make-To-Stock and Make-To-Order Strategic Hybrids
affiliations: Hellenic Open University, HSQ &Sustainability Division, Metlen Energy & Metals, University of Piraeus, Technical University Of Crete and Hellenic Open University

detail.title: How Much Customization Can a Production System Promise? The Case of Flow-Shops Under Make-To-Stock and Make-To-Order Strategic Hybrids
detail.abstract: Hybrid make-to-stock/make-to-order (MTS/MTO) production systems have emerged as a dominant response to mass customization. However, most existing research on hybrid flow shops revolves around scheduling and largely neglects the control problem of dynamically prioritizing capacity between standardized replenishment and customized order fulfillment under uncertainty. This paper addresses this gap by developing a control-oriented framework for stochastic parallel hybrid MTS/MTO flow shops with multiple stages and parallel machines. In particular, we consider an MTS-first hybrid architecture in which switching between MTS and multiple MTO customization classes incurs explicit setup costs and service performance is affected by finite buffers, stochastic demand and congestion propagation across stages. Methodologically, we integrate discrete-event simulation with a multi-output Machine Learning surrogate to construct a production-oriented stochastic meta-model. The computational results show that system-specific engineered features substantially improve surrogate accuracy across all evaluated models, with shallow multi-layer perceptrons achieving the best fidelity in reproducing both service level decrease and cost components. The results indicate that feasible customization levels are governed by coupled production and buffer capacities and that policies based only on feasibility can lead to excessive switching unless economic criteria are explicitly applied. Overall, the study advances the control theory of hybrid MTS/MTO flow shops by shifting the focus from sequencing to state-dependent prioritization and demonstrates how ML-based stochastic meta-models can support transparent, economically grounded decision rules in complex production environments.

detail.abstract: Short-horizon trader-support systems in financial markets should be judged not only by predictive skill but also by auditability, inspectability, and suitability for decision support under uncertainty. This paper studies an auditable 20-bar chart-image branch built from a retained MOEX Si futures artifact bundle. Starting from 14 contract-level one-minute candle files plus an auxiliary participant-position file, the pipeline resamples to 15-minute candles, selects the daily front contract by realized volume, applies a conservative liquidity filter, constructs a clean continuous-front series of 29,926 bars across 502 trading days, and generates 10,350 same-day, same-contract 20-bar windows rendered as 64 x 60 grayscale candlestick images. A three-block convolutional neural network (CNN) and a Grad-CAM-style local explanation layer are then embedded in a dashboard-centered inspection workflow. On the held-out test split (1,646 windows), the model attains 0.552 accuracy, 0.530 balanced accuracy, 0.408 F1, 0.557 ROC-AUC, and 0.063 MCC. Performance is modest and, at the default 0.50 threshold, trails the naive majority-class baseline on raw accuracy, while remaining better than random in threshold-free ranking terms. Results are contract-concentrated: SiZ5 materially outperforms SiU5. Quantitative explanation summaries show that heat mass is concentrated mainly in the price panel (0.807) rather than volume (0.193), but remains broad and only weakly focused on the final bar (0.043). The contribution is therefore bounded: not novelty of chart-image CNN forecasting or Grad-CAM in futures, both of which already exist, but the integration of chronology-aware futures engineering, auditable chart-image modeling, local explanation outputs, and row-level dashboard inspection in a trader-facing decision-support artifact. Fee-aware economic validation and formal user evaluation remain separated as pending next-stage work.

title: User Imprint: Psychological Profiling and Qualified Information in Prolonged Interaction with Large Language Models
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: User Imprint: Psychological Profiling and Qualified Information in Prolonged Interaction with Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Prolonged interaction with large language models (LLMs) produces a profiling effect that extends beyond commonly documented risks such as hallucinations, confirmation bias, or source fabrication. This paper identifies and formalises a phenomenon we propose to call user imprint: the LLM's ability to aggregate data disseminated across multiple interactions to build an exploitable psychological profile. This concept extends the surveillance capitalism framework (Zuboff, 2019) to a context in which data is no longer passively captured but actively delivered by the user, in what we term qualified information. An exploratory demonstration shows that an LLM, fed personality traits over weeks of conversation, can identify a fictitious user's psychological vulnerabilities and propose operational tactics to exploit them, without any spontaneous ethical reservation. Converging signals from industry practices-including Anthropic's memory migration tool launched in March 2026, which explicitly treats user imprint as a transferable asset-reinforce the plausibility of the phenomenon. This paper constitutes a theoretical proposition accompanied by a proof of concept, sufficiently defined to be subjected to experimental protocols and sufficiently grounded to warrant such investigation.

title: Decision Without Deciders: AI Governance and the Infrastructuralization of Accountability

detail.title: Decision Without Deciders: AI Governance and the Infrastructuralization of Accountability

detail.abstract: AI systems are transforming how consequential decisions are produced and how accountability is organized. Rather than functioning as tools operated by identifiable agents, algorithmic systems increasingly operate as decision environments in which outcomes emerge from distributed socio-technical configurations. This paper theorizes this transformation as responsibility absorption: the structural migration of accountability from traceable relations between agents and outcomes into infrastructural architectures, producing the condition of decision without deciders. In such systems, decisions occur without identifiable decisionmakers in the sense required for conventional accountability, not because responsibility disappears but because it is reconstituted as a systemic property of configuration rather than an attribute of agents. The paper develops a structural framework for understanding this transformation. It contrasts chain-based accountability models, which organize responsibility through discrete decisional acts and identifiable agents, with field-based decision structures, in which outcomes emerge from distributed configurations. It then theorizes responsibility absorption as the displacement of agency, authority, and normative responsibility into infrastructural systems. Accountability is subsequently reconceptualized as an infrastructural property-a characteristic of system architecture rather than a regulatory overlay imposed through oversight mechanisms. Building on this reconceptualization, the paper articulates three principles for embedding accountability within system architectures: binding authority to configuration, preserving foreclosed alternatives, and architectural contestability. Together, these principles define a model of structural placement in which responsibility is positioned within socio-technical systems rather than retrospectively attributed to individual actors. The paper concludes that AI governance cannot be adequately addressed through technical fixes, transparency mandates, or regulatory extensions of existing accountability frameworks. Instead, it requires the construction of accountability infrastructures-institutional architectures capable of rendering distributed configurations answerable in societies increasingly organized through infrastructural decision systems. AI governance is thus reframed not as the regulation of a technology but as the architectural design of decision environments in conditions of decision without deciders.

title: Talking in Generalities or Talking in Detail? The Role of Unconfirmed Customer Expectations in Reviewers' Online Expression
affiliations: , Harbin Institute of Technology and Harbin Institute of Technology

detail.title: Talking in Generalities or Talking in Detail? The Role of Unconfirmed Customer Expectations in Reviewers' Online Expression
detail.abstract: What online reviewers say about a product determines readers' understanding of the product before use. Thus, it is meaningful to understand the reasons behind reviewers' expressions. Given that review content is a consequence of the emotional and psychological interpretation of the reviewer's expectations and experience, this study aims to explore how expectation disconfirmation affects online reviewers' expressions. On the basis of data from online customer reviews in the Ctrip hospitality sector, this study verifies the effects of expectation disconfirmation on review breadth and depth with a correlated topic model and Shannon entropy. The findings reveal that review breadth decreases and review depth increases as expectation disconfirmation increases. Moreover, compared with reviewers' identity disclosure, reviewers' anonymity amplifies the effects of expectation disconfirmation on review breadth and review depth, whereas an increase in temporal distance between the dates of consumption and review attenuates these effects. Drawing upon expectation confirmation theory and persuasion theory, this study contributes to the understanding of reviewers' psychology and behaviors and provides implications for online communication in internet society.

title: Rule 12 (B) (6) As the Procedural Architecture of Artificial Intelligence Litigation in the United States

detail.title: Rule 12 (B) (6) As the Procedural Architecture of Artificial Intelligence Litigation in the United States
detail.abstract: This article conceptualizes Rule 12(b)(6) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as the central procedural mechanism structuring contemporary artificial intelligence litigation in the United States. It argues that the motion to dismiss no longer functions merely as a preliminary technical filter but as the constitutive stage at which a technological conflict acquires legal existence within federal adjudication.

detail.abstract: This study examines technology-driven social learning platforms such as crowdsourced customer support and the emergence of core–periphery knowledge-sharing network structures. We propose a dynamic structural model with endogenized knowledge-sharing and network formation that recognizes the dynamic and interdependent nature of knowledge seeking and sharing decisions. These decisions are driven by knowledge increments and social status building in anticipation of future reciprocal rewards from peers. Our model provides insights into how platform design can shape network structures to optimize knowledge sharing in online communities.

title: Third-Party Pricing Algorithms and Information Sharing
affiliations: and University of Rochester - Simon Business School

detail.title: Third-Party Pricing Algorithms and Information Sharing
detail.abstract: We analyze how the outsourcing of algorithmic pricing to a common third party influences the effects of information sharing in oligopoly. Algorithms enable competing firms to tailor prices to high-frequency demand shocks, and we compare regimes that either allow or prohibit conditioning on rival-specific shocks. We find that information sharing harms expected consumer surplus to a greater extent when pricing is outsourced to a common third party than when firms develop pricing algorithms in-house. Expected welfare rises with information sharing under in-house algorithm design but falls when pricing is outsourced, making third-party algorithms using rival demand information the worst regime for consumers and welfare.

title: Constitutional Logic in the Ethereum Virtual Machine: A Technical Implementation Report on Ternary Moral Logic

detail.title: Constitutional Logic in the Ethereum Virtual Machine: A Technical Implementation Report on Ternary Moral Logic

keywords: Zero-Knowledge Proofs Constitutional Logic in the Ethereum Virtual Machine: A Technical Implementation Report on Ternary Moral Logic

detail.abstract: Traditional smart contract architectures operate on binary determinism ("Code is Law"), resolving all transactions into valid or invalid states. This framework is insufficient for high-stakes governance and autonomous systems where ethical ambiguity requires a state of suspension rather than immediate execution. This paper presents the reference implementation of Ternary Moral Logic (TML) within the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM). We introduce a finite state machine that enforces a mandatory third state-the "Sacred Zero" or Epistemic Hold-enabling smart contracts to pause execution when pre-defined ethical conditions are unmet. The architecture utilizes EIP-712 typed data signing for cryptographic provenance, Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZK-SNARKs) for private verification, and a Dual-Lane Latency model to maintain high throughput for non-ambiguous transactions. Furthermore, we define an "Immutable Core" proxy pattern to eliminate administrative "God Mode" overrides, and demonstrate safety properties using TLA+ formal verification. This framework transforms the smart contract from a rigid automation tool into a constitutional enforcement layer capable of auditable, non-bypassable ethical hesitation.

title: A Dynamic Model of Rational Addiction: Evaluating Cigarette Taxes
affiliations: and Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: A Dynamic Model of Rational Addiction: Evaluating Cigarette Taxes
detail.abstract: Addiction creates an intertemporal link between a consumer's past and present decisions, altering their responsiveness to price changes relative to nonaddictive products. We construct a dynamic model of rational addiction and endogenous consumption to investigate how consumers respond to policy interventions that aim to reduce purchases of cigarettes. We find that, on average, the category elasticity is about 35% higher when the model correctly accounts for addiction. However, some policies spur substitution from more expensive single packs to less expensive cartons of cigarettes, resulting in higher overall consumption for some consumers. These findings have important implications for the design of tobacco taxation policy.

detail.abstract: Customers have predictable life cycles. As a result of these life cycles, firms that sell multiple products or services frequently observe that, in general, certain items are purchased before others. This predictable phenomenon provides opportunities for firms to cross-sell additional products and services to existing customers. This article presents a structural multivariate probit model to investigate how customer demand for multiple products evolves over time and its implications for the sequential acquisition patterns of naturally ordered products. Among the substantive findings are that women and older customers are more sensitive to their overall satisfaction with the bank than men and younger customers when determining whether to purchase additional products.

detail.abstract: This article examines whether brand-switching elasticities derived from logit choice models are overestimated as a result of rational consumer adjustment of purchase timing to coincide with promotion schedules and whether a dynamic structural model can address this bias. Using simulated data, the authors show that if the structural model is correct, brand-switching elasticities are overestimated by stand-alone logit models. A nested logit model improves the estimates but not completely. The dynamic structural model provides more accurate decomposition of promotional effects into brand switching, stockpiling, and consumption acceleration components.

title: A Dynamic Model of Health Insurance Choices and Healthcare Consumption Decisions
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, Virginia Tech - Pamplin College of Business, Carnegie Mellon University - David A. Tepper School of Business and Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: A Dynamic Model of Health Insurance Choices and Healthcare Consumption Decisions
detail.abstract: This paper examines data from a health insurer in the United States on the insurance plan and treatment options for chronically ill patients over a three-year period. Treatments vary widely in terms of cost and impact: expensive frontier treatments provide the best outcome for only the seriously ill, while cheaper, established treatments prove effective for most other patients. We develop a dynamic structural model to analyze how insurance plan generosity affects both insurance choice and healthcare consumption decisions. The findings show that generous health insurance plans encourage overtreatment but may not improve health outcomes, with important implications for insurance plan design and healthcare policy.

title: Are We Currently Experiencing the Fifth Industrial Revolution? The Case for Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Are We Currently Experiencing the Fifth Industrial Revolution? The Case for Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: Every Industrial Revolution in recorded history has been characterised by a singular enabling technology that restructured labour markets, reorganised production systems, and permanently altered the social and institutional architecture of society. This article advances the thesis that Artificial Intelligence (AI), encompassing large language models, generative AI systems, and autonomous agents that emerged in mature form between approximately 2017 and 2026, constitutes the defining technological catalyst of a Fifth Industrial Revolution. Drawing on historical analyses of prior industrial transitions, primary and peer-reviewed empirical literature, and current enterprise adoption data, the argument proceeds in four stages: (1) a definitional framework for what constitutes an industrial revolution is established from the historical record; (2) the four prior revolutions are mapped against this framework; (3) AI is evaluated against each criterion; and (4) the critical distinction between Industry 4.0 and Industry 5.0, a frequently conflated debate in both academic and practitioner discourse is resolved. The analysis concludes that AI meets every historical threshold for revolutionary classification and that this transition is not approaching but already underway.

title: The M.A.T.H. Framework: A First-Principles Approach to Quant Marketing in High-Uncertainty Environments

detail.title: The M.A.T.H. Framework: A First-Principles Approach to Quant Marketing in High-Uncertainty Environments
detail.abstract: The digital advertising ecosystem generates data volumes exceeding human cognitive processing capacity by orders of magnitude, while simultaneously degrading data quality through invalid traffic, attribution fragmentation, algorithmic opacity, and privacy-driven observational collapse. This paper formalizes the resulting structural mismatch, the Linear-Exponential Gap, between exponential growth in market complexity and approximately logarithmic growth in human analytical bandwidth. We introduce the M.A.T.H. Framework (Measure, Analyze, Tweak, Harvest), a recursive optimization protocol whose four stages address the principal failure modes of modern advertising operations: data corruption (Measure), confounded inference (Analyze), insufficient experimental velocity (Tweak), and suboptimal scaling (Harvest). We develop the information-theoretic foundations of each stage, including formalization of the data processing inequality as a bound on optimization performance, causal inference methods for deconfounding observational data, the Cycle Velocity construct for quantifying experimental throughput, and marginal economic analysis for identifying optimal scaling boundaries. System-level analysis demonstrates convergence properties governed by the Effective Learning Rate and degradation dynamics governed by creative fatigue, competitive displacement, and algorithmic drift. We establish conditions under which the framework achieves antifragility: converting environmental volatility into informational advantage. The framework operates on aggregate data rather than individual-level tracking, making it structurally compatible with privacy regulation and invariant to ongoing reductions in user-level observability.

title: Work from Home and Disability Employment
affiliations: ,  and University of Kalmar

detail.title: Work from Home and Disability Employment

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: There has been a dramatic rise in disability employment since the pandemic. At the same time, work from home (WFH) has risen four-fold. This paper asks whether the two are causally related. Controlling for compositional changes and labor market tightness, a 1 percentage point increase in WFH increases full-time employment by 1.0% for individuals with a physical disability. The postpandemic increase in working from home explains 68%-85% of the rise in full-time employment. Wage data suggests that WFH increased the supply of workers with a physical disability, likely by reducing commuting costs and enabling better control of working conditions.

detail.title: Why Is Manufacturing Productivity Growth So Low?

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Philadelphia Working Paper No. 26-19
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the recent slow growth in manufacturing productivity. We show that nearly all measured TFP growth since 1987 — and its post-2000s decline — comes from a few computer-related industries. We argue conventional measures understate manufacturing productivity growth by failing to fully capture quality improvements. We compare consumer to producer and import price indices. In rapidly changing industries, consumer price indices indicate less inflation, suggesting mismeasurement in standard industry deflators. Using an input-output framework, we estimate that TFP growth is understated by 1.4 percentage points in durable manufacturing and 0.3 percentage points in nondurable manufacturing and is slightly overstated in nonmanufacturing industries.
